1.   The CE marking shall be affixed visibly, legibly and indelibly to the product or to its data plate. Where that is not possible, or not warranted, on account of the nature of the product, it shall be affixed to the packaging and to the accompanying documents.
2.   The CE marking shall be affixed before the product is placed on the market.
3.   Member States shall build upon existing mechanisms to ensure correct application of the regime governing the CE marking and shall take appropriate action in the event of improper use of that marking.
CHAPTER VIII

content.text: Both claims **confirmed** against primary sources. Now the shipped files.

content.content:
1	# Access
2	
3	**This file exists because of a counted absence.**
4	
5	The three parent pipelines all marked accessibility a hard rule. Across roughly 5,000 lines of
6	combined instruction they contained **zero** mentions of ARIA, focus management, live regions, or
7	accessible names. Not one. That is not an oversight, and it is not a gap you close by being more
8	careful next time — it is the structural consequence of only ever *checking* accessibility in a
9	final pass and never *designing* it. A checklist can ask "is the contrast 4.5:1?" A checklist
10	cannot ask "should this be a grid or a table?", because by the time anyone runs it the answer is
11	already in the code.
12	
13	So `§10` is a hard rule, and this is the file that makes it enforceable. **Everything below is a
14	Loop 1 decision — made in `loops/01-direction.md`, written into `DIRECTION.md`, before a single
15	image is generated.** Not because auditing later is impossible; several of these are trivially
16	automatable, and `axe-core` will find them. Because the ones that matter are not defects to be
17	found. They are *shapes*: a non-drag affordance occupies layout space, a grid and a table are two
18	different keyboard experiences of the same visual, a VoiceOver grouping is a decision about what
19	is next to what. You do not fix those in Loop 8. You redraw.
20	
21	The `§16` rule applies here in one direction only. The human may skip any non-hard step at a
22	stated cost. `§10` is **[HARD]**. What is negotiable is *how much* of this file a given surface
23	needs — a static one-page portfolio does not owe a combobox decision. What is not negotiable is
24	deciding rather than discovering.
25	
26	---
27	
28	## The fork
29	
30	Read row 1 of `TRANSLATE.md` first. Both branches owe everything in this file. They owe it in a
31	different order, and they fail differently.
32	
33	**Page-shaped** — read for seconds, once. The failure mode is **structure**: no landmarks, a
34	heading order that follows visual weight instead of meaning, an icon-only social row with no
35	accessible names, motion nobody art-directed a still frame for. Almost always web, so WCAG binds
36	directly and `§10`'s keyboard-reachable-everything is the floor. The reader arrives once, from a
37	search result or a link, and either the page announces its own shape in the first three seconds
38	of screen-reader output or it does not. Sections 2, 3, 6, 8, 9 and 11 below are the ones that
39	decide it.
40	
41	**Tool-shaped** — read for hours, daily. The failure mode is **widgets**. Every hard problem in
42	this file lives here: a data grid, a combobox that filters 40,000 rows, a modal that has to
43	return focus to the row it came from, a queue that updates while the operator is typing
44	somewhere else. `§15` already demands full keyboard workflow completion and `TOOLS.md` spends
45	the budget — this file is where that same commitment gets its ARIA contract, because **picking a
46	widget pattern *is* picking a keyboard model** (§4 below), and the person who does this job eight
47	hours a day with a screen reader is the same person `§15` was written for. Sections 4, 5, 6 and
48	7 are the ones that decide it.
49	
50	**One asymmetry worth naming before you start.** A page-shaped surface can be made accessible
51	with almost no ARIA — native elements, real headings, `main`, `nav`, `alt`. A tool-shaped
52	surface cannot; composite widgets have no native equivalent. That is exactly why §5 below
53	matters more to the tool: the surface that *needs* ARIA is the surface where bad ARIA does the
54	most damage.
55	
56	---
57	
58	## 1. The operative target is WCAG 2.2 AA
59	
60	WCAG 2.2 is a W3C Recommendation (published 5 October 2023, republished 12 December 2024). It
61	adds nine success criteria over 2.1 and removes one — 4.1.1 Parsing — for **87 SCs against 2.1's
62	78**. Quoting "adds nine" without the removal produces a wrong count.
63	
64	WCAG 3.0 is a **Working Draft dated 3 March 2026**. Its own text says it "still has several years
65	of work" and that "It is inappropriate to cite this document as other than a work in progress."
66	It does not deprecate WCAG 2 — WAI's own intro page states WCAG 3 "will not supersede WCAG 2 and
67	WCAG 2 will not be deprecated for at least several years after WCAG 3 is finalized." No design
68	or procurement decision in 2026 anchors to WCAG 3.
69	
70	**And no law in force names 2.2 either** (§12 below). Section 508 names WCAG 2.0. The ADA Title
71	II rule names WCAG 2.1. The European Accessibility Act names no WCAG version at all. So designing
72	to 2.2 is **anticipatory, not compliance** — which is the honest framing and also the right
73	decision, because the gap between 2.1 and 2.2 is precisely the six new A/AA criteria in §2 below,
74	and every one of them is cheaper to decide in a comp than to retrofit into a shipped layout.
75	
76	Two version traps that catch people who half-remember the spec:
77	
78	- Earlier 2.2 drafts numbered 2.4.11 and 2.4.12 as "Focus Appearance (Minimum/Enhanced)". The
79	  final Recommendation uses **Focus Not Obscured** for 2.4.11 and 2.4.12, and a single **2.4.13
80	  Focus Appearance** at AAA. Drafts also had 2.4.13 at AA; it is not.
81	- **2.4.7 Focus Visible remains AA.** A persistent myth moves it to A. It did not move.
82	
83	One framing correction this file holds itself to. "These criteria cannot be retrofitted" is
84	overstated and this project has already caught itself saying it. `axe-core` ships an automated
85	`target-size` rule that measures both the size and the spacing routes; padding remediation is
86	routine; the 2.5.7 fix for a custom slider is click-anywhere-on-track, a pure implementation
87	change with no new UI. The defensible claim is narrower and it is the one that justifies Loop 1:
88	**several of these require new UI or new architecture** — an equivalent-control affordance, a
89	sticky-chrome geometry, an authentication method — **and those cannot be bolted on.** The rest
90	are simply cheapest when decided in the comp.
91	
92	---
93	
94	## 2. The six new A/AA criteria, as design decisions
95	
96	Six of WCAG 2.2's nine additions land at A or AA and are therefore in scope for an AA target:
97	2.4.11, 2.5.7, 2.5.8, 3.2.6, 3.3.7, 3.3.8. Each converts something that used to be implicit into
98	a measurable spec item. Each is answered in `DIRECTION.md`.
99	
100	A note on attribution that runs through this whole section: much of the most designer-useful
101	material lives in **Understanding** documents, which W3C labels "Informative explanations, not
102	required to meet WCAG." Where that is the case the phrasing below is "W3C guidance states"
103	rather than "the criterion requires." The distinction is not pedantry — a claim about what a
104	standard *requires* is checkable, and this project has already caught a summarizer inventing
105	normative wording twice.
106	
107	### 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), AA — 24×24 CSS px of *effective* area
108	
109	The measurement rule, from the Understanding doc's "Size requirement" section: a solid 24×24 CSS
110	px axis-aligned square must fit entirely inside the target. (Informative, not normative.)
111	
112	There are exactly five exceptions, and their names are worth knowing because summarizers
113	routinely merge two of them into a sentence that does not exist: **Spacing, Equivalent, Inline,
114	User Agent Control, Essential.**
115	
116	**"A hard 24px floor" is wrong.** The floor is on *effective, spacing-inclusive activation area*,
117	and it is satisfiable by size **or** by spacing.
118	
119	#### The spacing exception, with the geometry — the piece `SURFACES.md` defers here
120	
121	`SURFACES.md` names the second route and hands the geometry to this file. Here it is.
122	
123	Center a **24 CSS px diameter circle** on the bounding box of each undersized target. The target
124	passes the Spacing exception when that circle **does not intersect** either (a) another target,
125	or (b) the circle of another undersized target.
126	
127	Three consequences that fall straight out of the geometry and belong in the layout, not the QA:
128	
129	1. **Two adjacent undersized targets need 24 px centre-to-centre**, because two 24 px-diameter
130	   circles are disjoint exactly when their centres are 24 px apart. Not 24 px of gap — 24 px of
131	   *centre separation*. A 16 px icon with 8 px of gap between icons gives you 24 px centre to
132	   centre and passes; the same 16 px icon with 6 px of gap fails, and the visual difference is
133	   two pixels.
134	2. **The measurement is centre-to-centre in the plane, not per-axis.** A tightly packed grid of
135	   small controls can satisfy horizontal spacing and fail diagonally. Toolbars are safe; icon
136	   grids are where this bites.
137	3. **The circle is not the target.** A larger neighbour's actual bounding box counts against
138	   you even if that neighbour is comfortably over 24 px. A small close button tucked against a
139	   large primary action fails on the *primary action's* edge.
140	
141	This is a token decision and a layout decision, taken together, and it is why it lives in Loop 1:
142	it fixes a minimum spacing unit in the scale before any component is drawn.
143	
144	**The Inline exception is the one that gets over-specced.** It exempts links inside a sentence
145	and targets whose size is constrained by the line-height of non-target text. Applying a 24 px
146	minimum to prose links is not conformance, it is damage to the typography — and it is also the
147	part of 2.5.8 no automated checker can decide, because a checker cannot prove that line-height
148	constrains a target.
149	
150	**And the numbers do not transfer to native.** 24 CSS px is web- and pointer-scoped. Apple
151	publishes 44×44 pt *default* with a 28×28 pt *minimum*; Material publishes 48×48 dp for touch and
152	a separate, smaller 44×44 dp for pointer; WCAG's own AAA criterion 2.5.5 is 44×44. `SURFACES.md`
153	owns the full tables and the decision procedure. Do not carry 24 into a native design.
154	
155	### 2.5.7 Dragging Movements, AA — the affordance occupies layout space
156	
157	Normative text:
158	
159	> All functionality that uses a dragging movement for operation can be achieved by a single
160	> pointer without dragging, unless dragging is essential or the functionality is determined by
161	> the user agent and not modified by the author.
162	
163	**Satisfying the keyboard criteria does not satisfy this.** 2.1.1 and 2.1.3 are separate
164	obligations. The conforming fix is a *pointer-operable* control — a visible affordance that takes
165	up room in the layout — which is exactly why it is a concept-stage decision rather than a code
166	fix, for the class of interaction W3C itself names:
167	
168	> A sortable list of elements may, after tapping or clicking on a list element, provide adjacent
169	> controls for moving the element up or down
170	
171	> A task board that allows users to drag and drop items between columns also provides an
172	> additional pop-up menu after tapping or clicking
173	
174	> A map allows users to drag the view of the map around, and the map has up/down/left/right
175	> buttons.
176	
177	Reorder lists, kanban, map panning. If the design has any of those, the comp shows the buttons.
178	
179	**Two scope corrections, because this criterion is routinely over-claimed.** The user-agent
180	exception means native `<input type="range">` and native file-input drop behaviour are exempt —
181	only *custom* pointer-event sliders and *author-built* dropzones are in scope, and a drag-to-upload
182	zone usually already ships its alternative as the file input's Browse button. And for a custom
183	slider the conforming alternative is click-anywhere-on-track: a pure implementation change, no
184	new UI. Do not confuse 2.5.7 with 2.5.1 Pointer Gestures, which is about path-based gestures.
185	
186	W3C notes there are "very few situations in which dragging movements are essential." Assume yours
187	is not one of them.
188	
189	### 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), AA — sticky chrome creates an obligation
190	
191	At AA, the focused component must not be **entirely** hidden by author-created content. Partial
192	obscuring passes — the Understanding doc says so outright: "this AA criterion allows for the
193	component receiving focus to be partially obscured." The AAA sibling 2.4.12 forbids any part
194	being hidden.
195	
196	W3C names the offenders: "Typical types of content that can overlap focused items are sticky
197	footers, sticky headers, and non-modal dialogs" — and cookie banners explicitly: "A notification
198	implemented as sticky content, such as a cookie banner, will fail this success criterion if it
199	entirely obscures a component receiving focus." There is a dedicated failure technique, **F110**,
200	for sticky footers and headers.
201	
202	**The honest framing is not "sticky headers fail."** W3C says outright they "can be designed so
203	that they pass." The framing is: *choosing persistent chrome creates a paired geometric
204	obligation*, and the pair is decided together or not at all. The named passing designs:
205	
206	- Make the banner **modal**, so it must be dismissed before navigating the page.
207	- Use **CSS `scroll-padding`** so the banner never overlaps other content — this is a formally
208	  listed Sufficient Technique, **C43**, not prose advice.
209	- Close the notification **on loss of focus**.
210	
211	The list is explicitly open ("Ways of passing include"), so do not present it as exhaustive. Of
212	the three, only modal-versus-non-modal is a pure concept-time choice; `scroll-padding`'s
213	design-time counterpart is **"reserve layout space for persistent sticky chrome"** — which means
214	the sticky header's height is a number in the spacing scale, not a value someone picks in CSS
215	later.
216	
217	Two normative notes that cut the other way, and matter because they exempt a very common pattern:
218	only the **initial** position of user-repositionable content is tested, and content the user
219	opened that can be revealed or dismissed **without advancing focus** does not count as obscuring.
220	So a user-opened chat panel can be exempt while a persistent or auto-opening bubble is not.
221	"Floating chat widgets always fail" is wrong. Properly constructed modal dialogs always pass,
222	because they take focus.
223	
224	If a design goes for 2.4.13 Focus Appearance at AAA, note the number: an indicator at least as
225	large as a 2 CSS px thick perimeter of the component, with **3:1 contrast between the same pixels
226	in the focused and unfocused states** — not 3:1 against the background. That is an easy and
227	consequential misquote.
228	
229	### 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum), AA — the auth method is an architecture decision
230	
231	A cognitive function test is **not required** for any step in an authentication process unless
232	that step provides at least one of exactly four exceptions: **Alternative** (another method not
233	relying on a cognitive function test), **Mechanism** (something assists the user in completing
234	it), **Object Recognition**, or **Personal Content**. The AAA sibling 3.3.9 keeps only Alternative
235	and Mechanism.
236	
237	**Read that verb carefully.** The SC says such a test *is not required*; it does not forbid
238	offering one. W3C's Understanding page states it "does not forbid cognitive function tests
239	outright." "3.3.8 bans passwords" is a misreading — the Alternative exception is precisely what
240	converts *required* into *not required*. There is **no essentiality or security exception** in
241	3.3.8; a research summarizer once invented the wording "except where that test is essential to
242	the security of the content", which appears nowhere in the spec, and two claims stating the
243	exceptions that way were refuted outright.
244	
245	Normative **Note 2** — normative, not guidance — names the accepted Mechanism:
246	
247	> Examples of mechanisms that satisfy this criterion include: support for password entry by
248	> password managers to reduce memory need, and copy and paste to reduce the cognitive burden of
249	> re-typing.
250	
251	And the mechanism definition explicitly permits relying on the platform: "The mechanism may be
252	explicitly provided in the content, or may be relied upon to be provided by either the platform
253	or by user agents, including assistive technologies." You do not have to build it. You have to
254	not break it.
255	
256	**Which produces the rule with the sharpest edge in this entire file.** W3C guidance states:
257	
258	> if user agents and password managers are actively blocked from filling in the fields (for
259	> instance, by a script that prevents form fields from being automatically populated), or users
260	> are prevented from copy and paste operations (as they may rely on standalone/external third
261	> party password managers), then the page would fail this criterion unless an alternative is
262	> provided.
263	
264	**The security team's decision to disable paste on the password field is itself the accessibility
265	defect.** That argument was had and adjudicated: a 2021 W3C issue showed empirically, across four
266	operating systems, four browsers and five password managers, that "None of the tested combinations
267	generate/trigger a paste event" — blocking paste does not actually block extension-based managers.
268	The point was conceded and the published text was rewritten to justify the paste clause
269	independently, on behalf of users of standalone external managers. So this is not a live dispute
270	you can appeal to.
271	
272	Failure technique **F109** covers re-entry in a different format from creation — split OTP boxes,
273	"enter the 2nd, 6th and last characters" — and states that "A service that requires manual
274	transcription of a verification code is not compliant."
275	
276	The design decision, then, is architectural and it is made once: **offer passkeys, WebAuthn, or an
277	email link alongside the password path**, and the Alternative exception is satisfied for
278	everything downstream. Decide it in Loop 1 or discover it in a security review after the login
279	screen is built.
280	
281	### 3.3.7 Redundant Entry, Level A — multi-step flows
282	
283	**Level A, the lowest tier**, which routinely surprises people who assume the newer criteria are
284	all AA. Information previously entered by or provided to the user, required again **in the same
285	process**, is either **auto-populated or available for the user to select**. Three exceptions:
286	re-entering is essential, the information is required for security, or the previously entered
287	information is no longer valid.
288	
289	Two scoping precisions. The normative disjunction is *auto-populate or offer* — offering a prior
290	value to select is conforming, so this does not force autofill everywhere. And the scope is "in
291	the same process", where W3C defines a process as a sequence of activities toward one goal. W3C's
292	own plain-language summary loosely says "same session", which is looser than the normative text;
293	without "same process" a reader over-applies this across unrelated visits.
294	
295	For a tool-shaped surface this is the checkout criterion generalized: any multi-step flow, any
296	wizard, any create-then-configure sequence.
297	
298	### 3.2.6 Consistent Help, Level A — relative order, not position
299	
300	An earlier research pass established only this criterion's level and flagged the rest as an open
301	gap. Filled.
302	
303	What counts as a help mechanism, from the Understanding doc:
304	
305	> Typical help mechanisms include: Human contact details such as a phone number, email address,
306	> hours of operation. Human contact mechanism such as a messaging system, chat client, contact
307	> form, social media channel. Self-help option such as an up-to-date Frequently Asked Questions,
308	> How Do I page, Support page. A fully automated contact mechanism such as a chatbot.
309	
310	The requirement is **relative order across the set of pages**, not pixel position:
311	
312	> Regardless of which approach is used, the mechanism must be located in the same relative order
313	> on each page within the set of pages.
314	
315	> If the help item is visually in a different location, but in the same serial order, that is not
316	> helpful from a user's point of view, but it would not fail this criterion.
317	
318	It does **not** require help to exist: "It is not the intent of this success criterion to require
319	authors to provide help or access to help. The Criterion only requires that when one of the
320	listed forms of help is available across multiple pages that it be in a consistent location."
321	
322	The responsive exception is explicit and narrow — "This exception allows the location in a smaller
323	viewport to be different than in a larger viewport" — and **navigating between pages does not
324	qualify**: "merely navigating between pages within a set of web pages is not a 'change initiated
325	by the user' for the purposes of this exception."
326	
327	Sufficient technique **G220**, a contact-us link in a consistent location. Failure: *Inconsistent
328	Help Location*.
329	
330	The design consequence is small and specific: **help gets a fixed slot in the global template**,
331	decided once, and a mobile layout may move it as long as it stays in the same serial order.
332	
333	---
334	
335	## 3. Contrast — and the boundary that moves between platforms
336	
337	`§10` sets body contrast at **≥ 4.5:1**. That is WCAG 1.4.3 at AA and it is the floor, not the
338	target.
339	
340	The full AA set:
341	
342	| What | Ratio |
343	|---|---|
344	| Body text | **4.5:1** |
345	| Large text | **3:1** |
346	| UI components and graphical objects (1.4.11) | **3:1** |
347	
348	1.4.11 is the one design systems forget: an input border, a focus ring, a chart series, an
349	icon-only control's glyph, a toggle's off state. A 4.5:1 body rule with 1.5:1 input borders is a
350	common and complete failure — the text passes and the form is invisible.
351	
352	### The web/native boundary mismatch
353	
354	`SURFACES.md` flags this and hands it here.
355	
356	**The web's "large text" boundary is 18 px or 14 pt bold. Apple's is 17 pt.** Apple's own
357	Accessibility page cites both WCAG and APCA, then states what its tooling enforces:
358	
359	> Two popular standards of measure for color contrast are the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines
360	> (WCAG) and the Accessible Perceptual Contrast Algorithm (APCA). Accessibility Inspector uses the
361	> following values from WCAG Level AA.
362	
363	| Text size | Weight | Minimum ratio |
364	|---|---|---|
365	| Up to 17 pt | all | 4.5:1 |
366	| 18 pt | all | 3:1 |
367	| any | bold | 3:1 |
368	
369	**A design system that carries one contrast rule across web and iOS is using the wrong breakpoint
370	on one of them.** iOS body text is 17 pt by default — which sits on the *strict* side of Apple's
371	line, at 4.5:1, while a naive port of the web rule ("18px and up is large text") would relax
372	exactly the type that carries the most content. Set the boundary per platform in `DIRECTION.md`
373	and say which one you are using.
374	
375	### Contrast is a palette constraint, not a colour-picker step
376	
377	`§6` says sample the accent from the subject's real brand. That colour then has to *work*, and
378	whether it can carry body text, or only a 3:1 graphical role, or only a background, is a fact
379	about the colour — determined before it is placed, not adjusted afterwards. A brand accent that
380	cannot reach 4.5:1 on either background is not a problem to solve at the end; it is a constraint
381	on where the accent is allowed to appear, and that is a Loop 1 answer.
382	
383	Light and dark are two separate contrast systems. Verify both (`§12`). And the same icon needs a
384	different optical grade in each — Material publishes grade 0 for a dark icon on light, **−25** for
385	a light icon on dark, because of visual bleed. That is a light/dark obligation on the icon layer,
386	not just the colour layer.
387	
388	---
389	
390	## 4. ARIA pattern choice is a keyboard-model commitment
391	
392	This is the section the parent pipelines did not have a single line of, and the reason is
393	structural: pattern choice does not look like an accessibility question. It looks like an
394	implementation detail. It is not. **Choosing a pattern chooses a keyboard model, and the keyboard
395	model is visible in the design** — a grid needs a visible per-cell focus state, a menu needs an
396	open/closed affordance, a modal needs somewhere sensible for focus to land.
397	
398	The normative anchor, from WAI-ARIA 1.2 §4.3.1:
399	
400	> Authors MUST manage focus on the following container roles: grid, listbox, menu, menubar,
401	> radiogroup, tree, treegrid, tablist
402	
403	Eight roles. Reaching for any of them is signing up to write focus management. That is the cost
404	line, and it belongs in Gate B alongside the performance budget.
405	
406	### grid vs table — the same visual, two different keyboard experiences
407	
408	The single cleanest example in the APG, and the one most likely to be gotten wrong by a design
409	that never asked the question.
410	
411	| | `table` | `grid` |
412	|---|---|---|
413	| APG's own words | "A WAI-ARIA table is a static tabular structure… it is not an interactive widget." | "A grid widget is a container that enables users to navigate the information or interactive elements it contains using directional navigation keys" |
414	| Tab sequence | "**All** focusable elements contained in a table are included in the page tab sequence." | "**Only one** of the focusable elements contained by the grid is included in the page tab sequence." |
415	| Arrow keys | Nothing. Native scrolling. | Move between cells. |
416	
417	A 200-row table with a checkbox and two buttons per row is **600 tab stops** as a table and
418	**one** as a grid. Same pixels. That is not a code detail; it is the difference between a keyboard
419	user reaching row 200 in one keystroke and pressing Tab six hundred times.
420	
421	**And it is not simply "grid is better."** A grid is a composite widget: it puts a whole
422	interactive contract on you, and a data display with no interaction inside the cells is a table,
423	correctly. The decision procedure:
424	
425	- Cells contain **interactive controls** and the operator works *inside* the table for hours →
426	  **grid**. This is `TOOLS.md`'s data table. `§15` already demands arrows move, `Enter` opens,
427	  `Space` selects, `Shift` extends — that *is* the grid contract, so a tool-shaped surface has
428	  usually already committed.
429	- Cells are **read**, with at most a link per row → **table**. Reach for the native `<table>` and
430	  write no ARIA at all.
431	- Rows **expand and collapse** and cells are interactive → **treegrid**, which layers a hierarchy
432	  contract on top of grid: `aria-expanded` per row, Left/Right Arrow to collapse and expand.
433	
434	**The mode-switch trap**, which is where grid designs actually break. Any grid cell containing an
435	arrow-key-driven control — a combobox, a slider, a radio group — forces an explicit mode switch,
436	because grid navigation arrows and in-widget arrows cannot both own the arrow keys:
437	
438	> While navigation keys… are moving focus from cell to cell, they are not available to do
439	> something like operate a combobox… Enter: Disables grid navigation… Escape: restores grid
440	> navigation.
441	
442	That mode has to be **visible**. A cell that behaves differently depending on invisible state is a
443	bug for everyone, not only for screen-reader users, and drawing that state is a design job. If
444	the comp shows a dropdown inside a grid cell, the comp owes the entered-cell state too.
445	
446	*One claim deliberately not made here:* a plausible and frequently repeated line says grid puts
447	screen readers into application mode and therefore silently skips non-focusable cell content.
448	It was tested and did not survive verification. It is not in this file.
449	
450	### combobox — a closed choice of four, made at design time
451	
452	The popup is **not** an open design space. Per the normative spec it is one of exactly four
453	roles, and the choice is a `MUST`:
454	
455	> The popup is an element that has role listbox, tree, grid, or dialog
456	
457	Each carries a different keyboard contract, so the visual you draw determines the code:
458	
459	| Popup role | Keyboard, per APG | When |
460	|---|---|---|
461	| `listbox` | "Down Arrow moves focus to and selects the next option" | The ordinary case. Flat list of options. |
462	| `tree` | "Right Arrow… opens the node" | Hierarchical values — a category picker, a file path. |
463	| `grid` | "Down Arrow moves focus one cell down" | Multi-column results. A person picker with name, role and avatar in columns. |
464	| `dialog` | "Unlike other combobox popups, dialogs do not support `aria-activedescendant` so **DOM focus moves into the dialog**" | A date picker. Anything with its own internal controls. |
465	
466	The fourth row is the one that changes the design: **the dialog popup is the only one where real
467	focus leaves the input.** Draw a date picker inside a text field and you have committed to a focus
468	model different from the other three, including a return path.
469	
470	Plus a state obligation that is required by the normative ARIA spec, not merely APG guidance:
471	`aria-expanded` on the combobox element **must mirror the popup's visible open/closed state**.
472	Which means the design owes a visible open state — if the only cue that the popup is open is the
473	popup itself, there is nothing for the attribute to mirror.
474	
475	*Two adjacent claims were refuted 0-3 and are not repeated here:* that a combobox is defined by
476	presenting its value in an editable field the user can select and copy, and that combobox always
477	uses virtual focus via `aria-activedescendant`. The dialog case above disproves the second
478	outright.
479	
480	### menu / menubar — Tab exits
481	
482	> Tab and Shift + Tab do not move focus among the items in the menu… Each item in the menu has
483	> `tabindex` set to `-1`, except in a menubar, where the first item has `tabindex` set to `0`.
484	
485	Arrows navigate; **Tab leaves the whole widget**. The entire menu is one tab stop.
486	
487	Two more parts of the contract, non-optional: "When a menu opens, or when a menubar receives
488	focus, keyboard focus is placed on the first item", and "Escape: Close the menu that contains
489	focus and return focus to the element or context… from which the menu was opened."
490	
491	**Which means most things called "menus" should not use these roles.** A site navigation bar is a
492	list of links, and links belong in the tab sequence — making it a `menubar` removes six or eight
493	navigation links from Tab and gains nothing. The `menu` and `menubar` roles are for
494	**application menus**: the File/Edit/View bar of a tool, a right-click context menu, an actions
495	menu on a row. §5 below has the measured cost of getting this wrong, and it is the single
496	worst-performing pattern in the data.
497	
498	*One refuted claim, flagged because it sounds right:* that a submenu-opening item must expose a
499	persistent visible `aria-haspopup`/`aria-expanded` affordance. Voted down 0-3. Do not cite it.
500	
501	### modal dialog — one choice, four obligations
502	
503	Choosing "modal" bundles a contract:
504	
505	1. **Focus containment.** "Tab and Shift + Tab do not move focus outside the dialog… modal dialogs
506	   do not provide means for moving keyboard focus outside the dialog window without closing the
507	   dialog."
508	2. **Bidirectional transfer.** "When a dialog opens, focus moves to an element inside the dialog…
509	   When a dialog closes, focus returns to the element that invoked the dialog unless… the invoking
510	   element no longer exists." That last clause is the one tools hit: a modal that deletes the row
511	   it was opened from has no invoker to return to, and the design has to say where focus goes
512	   instead. `§15` states the rule; this is the edge case it does not cover.
513	3. **Initial focus is content-dependent** — a genuine design decision with three published
514	   answers: "add `tabindex="-1"` to a static element at the top of the dialog, such as the dialog
515	   title or first paragraph" for long or semantic content; "set focus on the least destructive
516	   action, especially if undoing the action is difficult or impossible"; the most-frequently-used
517	   action otherwise. Confirmation dialogs get Cancel, not Delete.
518	4. **`aria-modal="true"` is conditional**, and this is the one with real downside. Apply it only
519	   when the design enforces modality **both** behaviourally and visually:
520	
521	   > marking a dialog modal by setting `aria-modal` to true can prevent users of some assistive
522	   > technologies from perceiving content outside the dialog… mark a dialog modal only when both:
523	   > Application code prevents all users from interacting… Visual styling obscures the content
524	   > outside of it.
525	
526	   A "modal" with no scrim, that the page still scrolls behind, that sets `aria-modal="true"`, has
527	   hidden the entire page from assistive technology while remaining fully operable for everyone
528	   else. **The scrim is not decoration.** It is half of what makes the attribute honest.
529	
530	**One honest dissent to carry.** The focus-trap and focus-transfer items survived verification only
531	2-1. A published practitioner argument holds that focus-trapping is not strictly a WCAG normative
532	requirement and that the native `<dialog>` element plus `inert` achieves equivalent containment
533	without hand-rolled trap code. That challenges the *technique*, not the behavioural contract —
534	the user experience above is what has to happen either way, and the native route is very often
535	the right one. Which is `§10`'s "semantic structure or platform-native components", applied.
536	
537	### disclosure vs accordion — contested, and named as contested
538	
539	A disclosure controls one collapsible region and needs its trigger's `aria-expanded` kept in sync
540	with visibility (`aria-controls` is optional wiring, not the deliverable). An accordion is APG's
541	name for "a vertically stacked set of interactive headings that each contain a title", with a
542	**mandatory heading-role wrapper** on each button — so the discriminating signal APG actually
543	encodes in markup is *headedness*, meaning information architecture, meaning a design decision
544	about whether these sections are peers in a document outline.
545	
546	**The boundary is contested.** The claim above survived only 2-1, a W3C issue (`aria-practices`
547	#2445) is open on exactly this line with no editor resolution, and APG's own FAQ example
548	contradicts the "accordion = two or more disclosures" count-based heuristic that third-party
549	guidance uses. Two competing structural claims were refuted outright.
550	
551	So the rule here is not a boundary. It is: **pick one, and pick it for the content-structure
552	reason.** If the sections are peers in an outline, they are headed, and that is an accordion. If
553	one region toggles and owes nothing to a document structure, that is a disclosure. If a later
554	reader asks why, `DIRECTION.md` answers with the structure, not with a rule number — because the
555	rule number is not settled.
556

558	
559	## 5. The measured case for restraint
560	
561	Everything in §4 above argues that ARIA is a design decision. This section is why the default
562	answer to that decision is *less*.
563	
564	**WebAIM Million, 2026, approximately 1,000,000 home pages:**
565	
566	> Home pages with ARIA present had significantly more errors (**59.1** on average) than pages
567	> without ARIA (**42** on average)… Increased ARIA usage on pages was associated with higher
568	> detected errors. The more ARIA attributes that were present, the more detected accessibility
569	> errors could be expected.
570	
571	Roughly **41% more detected errors**, scaling with attribute count. And for one named pattern:
572	
573	> 5.7% of home pages had an ARIA menu (`role="menu"`), but **22% of those ARIA menus introduced
574	> accessibility barriers** due to the lack of necessary ARIA menu markup and interactions.
575	
576	More than one in five uses of `role="menu"` in the wild makes the page actively worse than doing
577	nothing. That is the pattern §4 above says is almost always the wrong choice for site navigation.
578	
579	**Cite this correctly.** WebAIM's own framing is that the relationship is **correlational, not
580	causal** — ARIA-heavy pages also tend to be more complex overall. The honest reading is not "ARIA
581	causes errors." It is that *ARIA is a promise, and promises are broken at scale.* APG puts it
582	directly:
583	
584	> `<div role="button">Place Order</div>` Is a promise that the author of that div has also
585	> incorporated JavaScript that provides the keyboard interactions expected for a button. Unlike
586	> HTML input elements, ARIA roles do not cause browsers to provide keyboard behaviors or styling.
587	> Using a role without fulfilling the promise of that role is similar to making a "Place Order"
588	> button that abandons an order and empties the shopping cart.
589	
590	**No ARIA is better than bad ARIA.** Which is a design rule, not a code rule, because the way a
591	design accumulates ARIA is by drawing things that have no native equivalent — a custom select
592	because the native one cannot be styled, a nav that looks like an application menu, a div that
593	looks like a button.
594	
595	The operating procedure, in order:
596	
597	1. **Can a native element do this?** `<button>`, `<a>`, `<details>`, `<dialog>`, `<table>`,
598	   `<input type="date">`. Free keyboard behaviour, free focus, free semantics, free platform
599	   updates. Every rung you climb from here costs a promise.
600	2. **Can a layout change remove the need?** Two disclosures instead of one tab widget. A visible
601	   filter row instead of a combobox. A second page instead of a modal. This rung is invisible to
602	   developers and available only at Loop 1 — which is the entire argument of this file in one
603	   line.
604	3. **Only then, a documented APG pattern**, with its keyboard contract written into
605	   `DIRECTION.md` as a cost.
606	
607	And the corollary that makes it enforceable: **an ARIA pattern in the design is a line item at
608	Gate B**, exactly like a shader's byte budget under `§11`. If it is not worth writing down, it is
609	not worth committing to.
610

612	
613	## 6. Focus
614	
615	`§15` owns the keyboard workflow. This section owns where focus *is*, which is a narrower and
616	harder problem.
617	
618	### The visible part
619	
620	Tab order follows visual order. Focus is always visible. Never trap focus except in a modal, and a
621	modal returns focus where it came from. All of that is `§15` and it is not restated here.
622	
623	What is added: **the focus indicator is a designed state, not `outline: auto`.** Removing the
624	default outline without replacing it is the most common single accessibility defect in
625	professionally designed interfaces, and it happens because the default is ugly and the replacement
626	was never drawn. Draw it. It needs 3:1 against adjacent colours (1.4.11), it must be visible on
627	every background it can land on including inside a dark modal over a light page, and if the design
628	goes to 2.4.13 at AAA it needs 3:1 between the focused and unfocused states of the same pixels.
629	
630	**`:focus-visible`, not `:focus`.** A mouse click on a button should not leave a ring; a Tab to it
631	must. The browser makes that distinction natively. Using it is one selector and it removes the
632	entire "the focus ring looks bad on click" argument that leads people to delete the ring.
633	
634	### Focus after the DOM changes — what the spec says, and where it stops
635	
636	WAI-ARIA 1.2 §4.3.1, normative:
637	
638	> If the author removes the element with focus, the author SHOULD move focus to a **logical
639	> element**. Similarly, authors SHOULD not scroll the element with focus off screen unless the
640	> user performed a scrolling action.
641	
642	That covers the tool-shaped cases directly, and each has a design answer that has to be written
643	down because "logical" is doing all the work:
644	
645	| The element with focus disappears because… | Where focus goes |
646	|---|---|
647	| The row it was in was deleted | The next row; the previous row if it was last; the table itself if empty |
648	| A modal closed | The invoker — and if the invoker is gone, a named fallback (see §4 above) |
649	| A filter emptied the list | The filter input, not the empty list |
650	| A step in a wizard advanced | The new step's heading, not the page top |
651	| An async load replaced the region | The region, if the user asked for it; nowhere, if they did not |
652	
653	For composite widgets there is a further normative-adjacent rule: when a previously focused
654	container is refocused, the active descendant should be **the same element** as when it was last
655	focused — with named exceptions for changed content and for menubar, "where the user expects to
656	always return to the first item."
657	
658	### The SPA route change — a specification gap, named as one
659	
660	A client-side route change is exactly the case the quote above describes: the element with focus
661	is removed. So the obligation applies.
662	
663	**What no W3C normative text specifies is the destination.** This was researched directly against
664	the primary sources rather than recalled, and the finding is that the specification is silent —
665	not that the lookup failed. There is no normative answer to where focus goes on a route change,
666	whether the new title must be announced, or how the View Transitions API interacts with focus
667	restoration.
668	
669	The consequence is not "so it does not matter." It is the opposite: **it is a decision, it is
670	yours, and it goes in `DIRECTION.md`** rather than being inherited from whatever the router does
671	by default. The default, in most frameworks, is that focus falls to `<body>` — which means the
672	next Tab starts at the top of the browser chrome and a screen reader announces nothing at all. An
673	interface where every navigation silently resets a keyboard user to zero has failed `§15`
674	completely, and no automated checker will report it, because nothing is technically wrong.
675	
676	Whatever you choose, choose it once and apply it to every route. And verify it the way `§12`
677	demands — navigate, then Tab, and watch where the ring appears.
678

681	## 7. Live regions
682	
683	The pattern nobody draws, because there is nothing to draw: **a message that arrives when the
684	user is looking somewhere else.** WAI-ARIA's own definition makes the design problem explicit:
685	
686	> Live regions are perceivable regions of a web page that are typically updated as a result of an
687	> external event **when user focus may be elsewhere**.
688	
689	Every tool-shaped surface has them. Saved. Sync failed. Three new jobs in the queue. 40 results.
690	Every one of those is visible to a sighted operator by peripheral vision and invisible to everyone
691	else unless a designer decided it should be announced.
692	
693	### The three values, verbatim, and the one that is dangerous
694	
695	> **assertive** — Indicates that updates to the region have the highest priority and should be
696	> presented the user immediately.
697	>
698	> **off (default)** — Indicates that updates to the region should not be presented to the user
699	> unless the user is currently focused on that region.
700	>
701	> **polite** — Indicates that updates to the region should be presented at the next graceful
702	> opportunity, such as at the end of speaking the current sentence or when the user pauses typing.
703	
704	The restraint clause is normative, with a `SHOULD NOT`:
705	
706	> Because an interruption may disorient users or cause them to not complete their current task,
707	> authors **SHOULD NOT use the assertive value unless the interruption is imperative**.
708	
709	`assertive` may also destroy queued speech: "User agents or assistive technologies MAY choose to
710	clear queued changes when an assertive change occurs." An assertive toast firing while a screen
711	reader is mid-sentence in a form field does not add a message. It **deletes** one.
712	
713	### `alert` vs `status` — the roles, and what they already imply
714	
715	| | `role="alert"` | `role="status"` |
716	|---|---|---|
717	| Spec description | "A type of live region with important, and usually time-sensitive, information." | "A type of live region whose content is advisory information for the user but is not important enough to justify an alert, often but not necessarily presented as a status bar." |
718	| Implicit `aria-live` | `assertive` | `polite` |
719	| Implicit `aria-atomic` | `true` | `true` |
720	
721	Both roles bring their politeness with them, so `role="alert" aria-live="assertive"` is redundant
722	and `role="alert" aria-live="polite"` is a contradiction someone will eventually have to debug.
723	
724	`status` carries one extra normative obligation, and it is a *design* one: "Authors SHOULD ensure
725	an element with role `status` does not receive focus as a result of change in status." A status
726	message that steals focus is a status message that interrupts the task it is reporting on.
727	
728	Two more live-region roles exist and are almost always misapplied: `log` ("new information is
729	added in meaningful order and old information may disappear" — a chat transcript, a build output)
730	and `marquee` ("non-essential information changes frequently" — a ticker). `timer` is one too.
731	
732	### The design decision, which is a triage
733	
734	For every asynchronous state change the surface can produce, decide once:
735	
736	| Class | Announcement | Example |
737	|---|---|---|
738	| Silent | none | Hover previews, purely cosmetic transitions, anything the user is already looking at |
739	| Advisory | `status` / polite | Saved. 40 results. Copied. Uploading, 60%. |
740	| Imperative | `alert` / assertive | Session expiring in 60 seconds. Payment failed. Data loss imminent. |
741	
742	The list is short on purpose. **The default is silent.** A surface that announces everything is a
743	surface a screen-reader user turns off, and there is no setting between "all of it" and "none of
744	it" that they control.
745	
746	`TOOLS.md` sets the visual side of this — where toasts appear, how long they persist. This is the
747	audio side, and the two are decided together: a toast that vanishes in three seconds and a polite
748	live region that waits for a graceful pause can miss each other entirely.
749	
750	### Where this stops being verified
751	
752	The politeness values are **"a strong suggestion"**, per the spec: "The value may be overridden by
753	user agents, assistive technologies, or the user." So the behaviour above is what you are asking
754	for, not what will happen.
755	
756	Two things you may have read that this file does **not** assert, because neither could be
757	confirmed against a primary source in this pass: that a live region must exist in the DOM before
758	content is injected into it (widely repeated, not in the WAI-ARIA 1.2 text), and any specific
759	account of how NVDA, JAWS and VoiceOver differ (no support table was verified). Both are marked
760	*not established in this pass — verify before relying on either.* They are also both reasons the
761	same rule applies as everywhere: `§12`, test it with an actual screen reader.
762

764	
765	## 8. Accessible names
766	
767	`§10` demands descriptive alt text on every image. This is the general case, and it is broader
768	than images: **every interactive element has a name, whether or not anyone chose it.** If nobody
769	chose it, the browser computes one from whatever is lying around, and the result is usually the
770	file name of an icon.
771	
772	The APG's five rules compress to three that are design decisions:
773	
774	> **Rule 2: Prefer Visible Text.** In addition to serving as a more robust source for an accessible
775	> name, visible text labels enhance accessibility for many people with disabilities who do not use
776	> assistive technologies that present invisible accessible names. In most circumstances, visible
777	> text labels also make the user interface easier to understand for all users.
778	
779	> **Rule 4: Avoid Browser Fallback.** … the HTML `title` and `placeholder` attributes are used as
780	> last resort sources of content for accessible names. Because the purpose of these attributes is
781	> not naming, their content typically yields **low quality accessible names that are not
782	> effective**.
783	
784	> **Rule 5: Compose Brief, Useful Names.** Similar to how visually crowded screens and ambiguous
785	> icons reduce usability, excessively long, insufficiently distinct, or unclear accessible names
786	> can make a user interface very difficult, or even impossible, to use for someone who relies on a
787	> non-visual form of the user interface.
788	
789	Rule 2 is the design one and it points at a layout choice: **a visible label is the accessible
790	name.** Every time the design removes a visible label — a placeholder instead of a label, an icon
791	instead of a word, a tooltip instead of a caption — it creates an invisible-name obligation that
792	someone has to remember. The cheapest accessible name is the one that is already on the screen.
793	
794	Rule 4 names the specific trap: `title`, "commonly presented visually as a tooltip when the user
795	hovers over the element with a pointing device, which is **not particularly discoverable, and is
796	also not accessible to visual users without a pointing device**." A tooltip is not a label. It is
797	invisible to touch, invisible to keyboard, and it disappears.
798	
799	Rule 5 is why "Read more" repeated eleven times fails: names must be **distinct**, because a
800	screen-reader user can pull up a list of every link on the page and eleven identical entries is
801	eleven identical entries.
802	
803	### The warning that silently deletes content
804	
805	Eighteen roles take their accessible name from their own child content — `button`, `cell`,
806	`checkbox`, `columnheader`, `gridcell`, `heading`, `link`, `menuitem`, `menuitemcheckbox`,
807	`menuitemradio`, `option`, `radio`, `row`, `rowheader`, `switch`, `tab`, `tooltip`, `treeitem`. On
808	any of them:
809	
810	> If an element with one of the above roles that supports naming from child content is named by
811	> using `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`, content contained in the element and its descendants is
812	> **hidden from assistive technology users** unless the descendant content is referenced by
813	> `aria-labelledby`. It is strongly recommended to avoid using either of these attributes to
814	> override content of one of the above elements except in rare circumstances where hiding content
815	> from assistive technology users is beneficial.
816	
817	A card that is one big `<a>` containing a heading, a summary and a date, given
818	`aria-label="Read the article"`, has just deleted the heading, the summary and the date. The
819	attribute does not add a label. It **replaces** the content.
820	
821	### Icon-only controls — the most common icon accessibility failure
822	
823	`icons-verified.md` flagged this explicitly as unchecked against a primary source. It is checked
824	now, and the rule is not the obvious one.
825	
826	W3C's tutorial on functional images:
827	
828	> Functional images are used to initiate actions rather than to convey information. They are used
829	> in buttons, links, and other interactive elements. **The text alternative for the image should
830	> convey the action that will be initiated (the purpose of the image), rather than a description
831	> of the image.**
832	
833	> For instance … the text alternative should be “print this page” rather than “(image of a)
834	> printer”, “search” rather than “magnifying lens” …
835	
836	**Name the action, not the picture.** A magnifying glass is not called "magnifying glass" or
837	"search icon" — it is called "Search". A trash can is "Delete", not "trash". A three-dot glyph is
838	"More actions for [the thing]", not "ellipsis" and not "menu".
839	
840	And the failure mode, stated by W3C rather than inferred:
841	
842	> Missing or empty alt values create significant problems for screen reader users because
843	> functional images are essential to the functionality of the content. Screen readers will
844	> typically announce the **image file name, the image URL, or the URL for the link destination**,
845	> which is unlikely to help users understand the action that will be initiated by the image.
846	
847	A row of five unnamed icon buttons is announced as five file names. That is the actual output, and
848	it is worse than nothing because the user cannot tell it is broken.
849	
850	Three more rules that come off the same sources:
851	
852	- **An icon that duplicates adjacent text takes `alt=""`.** W3C's own example: a logo image inside
853	  a link whose text already says where it goes gets a null alt, "to avoid redundancy and
854	  repetition." Naming both produces doubled speech.
855	- **Below 20 dp, a complex or key-action icon owes a *visible* text label** — Material's rule, and
856	  it is a design-time rule rather than a screen-reader patch. Navigation items always need labels.
857	- **Every custom glyph needs an accessible name on native too.** Apple states it on both the SF
858	  Symbols and Icons pages: "Provide alternative text labels for custom interface icons.
859	  Alternative text labels — or accessibility descriptions — aren't visible, but they let VoiceOver
860	  audibly describe what's onscreen."
861	
862	The Loop 1 output is small and concrete: **for every icon-only control in the design, the string.**
863	Not a note that says "add aria-labels" — the actual words, written next to the icon in the comp.
864	
865	### Names are content, and content gets translated
866	
867	Stated on the APG page itself: "When a user interface is translated into multiple languages, ensure
868	that `aria-label` values are translated." An accessible name is a string a human reads. It goes
869	through the same pipeline as every other string (§11 below), and an untranslated `aria-label` is a
870	control that speaks English inside a German interface.
871

873	
874	## 9. Structure — the part that costs nothing and is skipped anyway
875	
876	Landmarks and headings are the cheapest accessibility work available and the most commonly
877	missing, because they are invisible. A page-shaped surface lives or dies here.
878	
879	From the APG's landmark practice, as design rules:
880	
881	- **One `main` per page.** One `banner`, one `contentinfo`. Top-level.
882	- **"A region landmark must have a label."** It is the only landmark with a hard label
883	  requirement, and it exists to cover "content that named landmarks do not appropriately
884	  describe" — which means every time the design invents a major section that is not nav, main,
885	  aside or footer, that section owes a name.
886	- **More than one landmark of a type → each needs a unique label.** Two `nav` elements are "Main"
887	  and "Footer", not two anonymous navs.
888	- **And the inverse, which nobody encodes:** "If a navigation landmark has an identical set of
889	  links as another navigation landmark on the page, **use the same label** for each navigation
890	  landmark." A mobile nav and a desktop nav holding the same links share a name. Distinguishing
891	  them tells the user there are two navigations when there is one.
892	- A `form` landmark "should have a label … visible to all users (e.g. an `h1`–`h6` element)". Use
893	  `search`, not `form`, when it is a search.
894	
895	**The nesting trap.** HTML `header` and `footer` are landmarks *only when their context is the body
896	element*. Inside `article`, `aside`, `main`, `nav` or `section` they are not. So a layout decision
897	— wrapping the page in a `<section>` for styling — silently deletes the banner and contentinfo
898	landmarks, with no visual change and no error anywhere.
899	
900	**Headings are an outline, not a type scale.** `h1` through `h6` describe document structure;
901	`STYLES.md` describes size. A heading chosen because it is the right size is a broken outline, and
902	screen-reader users navigate by heading more than by any other mechanism. One `h1`. No skipped
903	levels. If the design needs a small heading in a prominent place, that is a CSS class, not an
904	`h5`.
905	
906	**Skip link.** One "Skip to content" link, first in the tab order, visible on focus. It is four
907	lines and it is the difference between reaching the article in one keystroke and forty.
908

911	## 10. Native — and where a web checklist misses
912	
913	`SURFACES.md` owns the platform tables. This section owns the places where a web-trained
914	accessibility instinct produces the **wrong answer** on native, which is a shorter and more useful
915	list.
916	
917	### The cleanest divergence found: system zoom
918	
919	Apple's guidance:
920	
921	> Ideally, give people the option to enlarge text by at least **200 percent** (or **140 percent**
922	> in watchOS apps).
923	
924	Apple's own word is "Ideally" — aspirational in the HIG. App Store Connect converts the same
925	numbers into pass/fail evaluation criteria for the Larger Text accessibility label, so it is a
926	shipping bar in practice.
927	
928	**And Apple explicitly excludes system Zoom and Hover Text from counting toward it.** The app must
929	enlarge its own text, via Dynamic Type or custom UI. System magnification does not satisfy the
930	requirement.
931	
932	**On the web, browser zoom does satisfy WCAG 1.4.4 Resize Text and 1.4.10 Reflow.** It is an
933	accepted mechanism.
934	
935	Same user-facing feature. Opposite verdict, depending on platform. There is no principle that
936	reconciles them and no way to derive one from the other — you have to know which platform you are
937	on. This is the single clearest reason a web-derived accessibility checklist cannot be pointed at
938	a native app.
939	
940	**What it costs the layout**, since 200% is not a font setting but a stack-axis change. Apple's
941	Dynamic Type ramp is 7 standard sizes plus 5 accessibility sizes, AX1 through AX5 — twelve sizes a
942	layout must survive. Body runs **17 pt to 53 pt**, roughly 3.1×, crossing 200% already at AX3.
943	Scaling is **non-uniform**: Large Title runs 34 pt to 60 pt, about 1.76×, so at the top of the ramp
944	Body nearly equals default-size Headline and *exceeds* default Large Title. Every size relationship
945	in the type scale inverts. Apple's stated remedies are layout instructions, not typography ones:
946	switch side-by-side layouts to a vertical stack so each element gets full width, let text wrap to
947	two or more lines rather than truncate, reduce multi-column text to fewer columns.
948	
949	Android 14 raised its own maximum to 200% with a **non-linear** curve so large text scales less
950	aggressively than small text. The consequence has no CSS analogue: **`sp` values stop being
951	additive.** 4 sp + 20 sp may not equal 24 sp, so `sp` must not be used for padding or for view
952	heights that assume implicit padding — and an app must be explicitly retested at 200% even though
953	`sp` gets the improvement automatically.
954	
955	### VoiceOver grouping is a layout-time decision
956	
957	Reading order is derived from layout: top to bottom, left to right in the user's active locale.
958	Which means an ungrouped gallery of images with captions is read as **every image, then every
959	caption** — two disjoint streams.
960	
961	Apple states this at the design-guideline level and defers the API to developer docs: "Specify how
962	elements are grouped, ordered, or linked." **Visual proximity encodes relationship silently.** A
963	sighted user sees the caption under the photo and the relationship is free. Nobody else gets it
964	unless a designer declared it.
965	
966	The Loop 1 output: audit the comp for every relationship conveyed *only* by proximity or
967	alignment, and write down which elements are one unit. That is a design artefact — it is the same
968	grouping decision as `STYLES.md`'s spacing, made explicit.
969	
970	### Label and value are separate channels
971	
972	Apple's VoiceOver evaluation criteria require a label distinct from a control's value: the label
973	names the field ("phone number"), the value carries the content ("555-0100"). And separately,
974	control type and state — "checkbox", "checked" — belong in **traits**, never in the label, because
975	duplicating them produces doubled speech: *checkbox, checkbox*.
976	
977	The web analogue is real and worth stating: an input's `<label>` is its name, its content is its
978	value, and `aria-label="Search field text input"` produces *search field text input, edit text*.
979	Name the thing. The platform announces what kind of thing it is.
980	
981	### Reduce Transparency and Increase Contrast are designed states
982	
983	`SURFACES.md` establishes that Liquid Glass re-renders under these settings and hands the
984	consequence here.
985	
986	They are **designed states**, exactly the way `§10` treats `prefers-reduced-motion`: a still frame
987	someone art-directed, not a degradation discovered in QA. A design whose hierarchy depends on
988	translucency has no hierarchy under Reduce Transparency. A palette tuned for subtlety has no
989	distinctions under Increase Contrast.
990	
991	So a native surface owes **three** designed states, not one, and `§12` applies to all of them —
992	screenshot each:
993	
994	| State | What it changes | Who it is for |
995	|---|---|---|
996	| Reduced motion | Transitions, parallax, autoplay | Vestibular disorders, motion sensitivity |
997	| Reduce Transparency | Materials become opaque; blur is removed | Low vision, cognitive load |
998	| Increase Contrast | Borders appear, colours separate, subtlety is destroyed | Low vision |
999	
1000	Apple also names the reduced-motion techniques rather than just the setting, and they are design
1001	instructions: tighten animation springs to reduce bounce; track animations directly with people's
1002	gestures; avoid animating depth changes in z-axis layers; replace transitions in x-, y- and z-axes
1003	with fades; avoid animating into and out of blurs. The last two are the ones that get missed, and
1004	they are exactly what is fashionable.
1005	
1006	### Four more native obligations with no web equivalent
1007	
1008	- **Gesture alternatives are mandatory.** "If you use a swipe gesture to dismiss a view, also make
1009	  a button available." A swipe-only interaction is a design defect. This is the native analogue of
1010	  WCAG 2.5.7, and it is broader — it covers any gesture, not only dragging.
1011	- **Time-boxed UI.** "Views and controls that auto-dismiss on a timer can be problematic… Prefer
1012	  dismissing views with an explicit action." A three-second toast carrying the only copy of an
1013	  Undo affordance is a defect.
1014	- **Assistive Access** (iOS/iPadOS) is a distinct layout mode to plan for: identify core
1015	  functionality, one interaction per screen, confirm twice on hard-to-recover actions.
1016	- **Accessibility Nutrition Labels** exist on the App Store. Accessibility support is now publicly
1017	  declared, which moves it from an internal quality bar onto a marketing surface — and makes an
1018	  overclaim a different kind of problem.
1019	
1020	One convenience worth knowing: SF Symbols "provides many variants for specific languages and
1021	writing systems, including Latin, Arabic, Hebrew, Hindi, Thai, Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Cyrillic,
1022	Devanagari, and several Indic numeral systems", and they "adapt automatically when the device
1023	language changes." That is `§13` handled at the icon layer, for free, on one platform. Custom
1024	glyphs get none of it — an arrow you drew yourself does not flip for RTL unless you draw the
1025	flipped one, which Apple states directly: "include a flipped version of the icon to use when the
1026	context is right-to-left."
1027	
1028	---
1029	
1030	## 11. Internationalization
1031	
1032	`§13` is the hard part and it is already stated: if the subject is presented in a non-Latin script
1033	or an RTL language, handle it properly — `dir="rtl"`, CSS logical properties, a font that actually
1034	renders the script, mirrored layout, **and never transliterate or mangle a name to make it fit.**
1035	That last clause is not a technical rule; it is the same respect `§14` extends to a face.
1036	
1037	This section adds what the parents lacked, which is everything that breaks a layout *before*
1038	anyone reaches a different script.
1039	
1040	### Text expansion — a real table, and its actual provenance
1041	
1042	W3C's i18n article republishes IBM's figures for English into European languages:
1043	
1044	| No. of characters in English source | Average expansion |
1045	|---|---|
1046	| Up to 10 | **200–300%** |
1047	| 11–20 | 180–200% |
1048	| 21–30 | 160–180% |
1049	| 31–50 | 140–160% |
1050	| 51–70 | 151–170% |
1051	| Over 70 | **130%** |
1052	
1053	**Attribution matters here.** These are IBM's numbers, republished by W3C as "average expected
1054	expansion rates" — not a W3C requirement and not a measurement of your strings. The 51–70 row is
1055	reproduced as published, above the preceding row's ceiling; that is what the source shows, and
