1	# Verified — legal enforcement, focus management, live regions, accessible names, i18n
2	
3	**Date:** 2026-08-02
4	**Method:** rendered DOM text pulled with a headless browser from the primary source itself,
5	then read in context. **Not** WebFetch summaries and **not** from memory. This project has
6	already caught four instances of plausible-but-wrong content, including one claim that
7	contradicted its own cited source, so every quote below was read off the live rendered page.
8	`curl` is useless for most of these: EUR-Lex and the W3C TR pages are JS-rendered and return a
9	near-empty shell to a plain fetch.
10	
11	**Why this pass exists.** Two areas returned **zero surviving claims across three separate
12	research-workflow attempts**: legal enforcement (`accessibility-wcag.md` finding 10 at *medium*
13	confidence and explicitly flagged "MUST be re-verified against the primary texts";
14	`native-a11y-verified.md` HALF TWO, zero claims) and SPA focus management / live regions
15	(`web-a11y-patterns.md` finding 8, zero claims). Law and spec sites defeat summarizers. The
16	browser is what works.
17	
18	**The rule this file is written under:** a wrong compliance deadline in a design tool is worse
19	than an absent one, because someone could rely on it. Everything not verified below is named
20	in the final section as *not established in this pass*, and nothing there ships as fact.
21	
22	Pages read:
23	
24	| Source | URL |
25	|---|---|
26	| Directive (EU) 2019/882 — European Accessibility Act | `https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32019L0882` |
27	| DOJ — ADA Title II web rule guidance | `https://www.ada.gov/resources/2024-03-08-web-rule/` |
28	| US Access Board — Revised Section 508 Standards (ICT) | `https://www.access-board.gov/ict/` |
29	| WAI-ARIA 1.2 (Recommendation) | `https://www.w3.org/TR/wai-aria-1.2/` |
30	| ARIA APG — Landmark Regions | `https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/practices/landmark-regions/` |
31	| ARIA APG — Providing Accessible Names and Descriptions | `https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/practices/names-and-descriptions/` |
32	| WAI Tutorial — Functional Images | `https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/images/functional/` |
33	| Understanding SC 3.2.6 Consistent Help | `https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/consistent-help.html` |
34	| W3C i18n — Text size in translation | `https://www.w3.org/International/articles/article-text-size` |
35	| W3C i18n — Approaches to line breaking | `https://www.w3.org/International/articles/typography/linebreak.en` |
36	| Unicode CLDR — Plural Rules | `https://cldr.unicode.org/index/cldr-spec/plural-rules` |
37	
38	The ADA page carries a dateline of **April 08, 2024** with the April 2026 extension folded into
39	its opening paragraph. EUR-Lex serves the consolidated directive text. W3C pages carry a 2026
40	copyright line.
41	
42	---
43	
44	## 1. The European Accessibility Act — Directive (EU) 2019/882
45	
46	### The dates, verbatim from Article 31
47	
48	> 1.   Member States shall adopt and publish, by 28 June 2022, the laws, regulations and
49	> administrative provisions necessary to comply with this Directive. They shall immediately
50	> communicate the text of those measures to the Commission.
51	>
52	> 2.   They shall apply those measures from **28 June 2025**.
53	>
54	> 3.   By way of derogation from paragraph 2 of this Article, Member States may decide to apply
55	> the measures regarding the obligations set out in Article 4(8) at the latest from 28 June 2027.
56	
57	Article 2 scopes the same date to the goods and services themselves — products "placed on the
58	market **after 28 June 2025**", services "provided to consumers **after 28 June 2025**".
59	
60	**Article 32 is the part almost every summary drops.** There is a long transitional tail:
61	
62	> Member States shall provide for a transitional period ending on **28 June 2030** during which
63	> service providers may continue to provide their services using products which were lawfully
64	> used by them to provide similar services before that date.
65	>
66	> Service contracts agreed before 28 June 2025 may continue without alteration until they
67	> expire, but no longer than **five years** from that date.
68	
69	Self-service terminals lawfully in use before 28 June 2025 may run "until the end of their
70	economically useful life, but no longer than **20 years** after their entry into use."
71	
72	So "the EAA applied from 28 June 2025" is true and incomplete: legacy content and legacy
73	hardware have their own clocks running to 2030 and beyond.
74	
75	### What is actually in scope
76	
77	Products (Article 2(1)): consumer general-purpose computer hardware systems and their operating
78	systems; payment terminals; ATMs, ticketing machines, check-in machines and interactive
79	self-service information terminals; consumer terminal equipment with interactive computing
80	capability used for electronic communications services; the same for accessing audiovisual media
81	services; and e-readers.
82	
83	Services (Article 2(2)): electronic communications services; services providing access to
84	audiovisual media services; named elements of air, bus, rail and waterborne passenger transport
85	(websites, mobile apps, e-tickets, travel information, interactive self-service terminals);
86	**consumer banking services**; **e-books and dedicated software**; and **e-commerce services**.
87	Article 2(3) adds answering emergency communications to 112.
88	
89	Content exempted from the website/app obligations includes "pre-recorded time-based media
90	published before 28 June 2025", "office file formats published before 28 June 2025", and
91	archives containing only content not updated or edited after 28 June 2025.
92	
93	### The microenterprise exemption, with its actual threshold
94	
95	Article 3 definition, verbatim:
96	
97	> ‘microenterprise’ means an enterprise which employs **fewer than 10 persons** and which has an
98	> annual turnover **not exceeding EUR 2 million** or an annual balance sheet total not exceeding
99	> EUR 2 million;
100	
101	Article 4(5), verbatim:
102	
103	> Microenterprises providing services shall be exempt from complying with the accessibility
104	> requirements referred to in paragraph 3 of this Article and any obligations relating to the
105	> compliance with those requirements.
106	
107	Note the asymmetry, which is stated in Recital: microenterprises **providing services** are
108	exempt outright; microenterprises **dealing with products** are not exempt — their obligations
109	are merely "lighter", and Article 14(4) exempts them only from *documenting* their
110	disproportionate-burden assessment, not from making it.
111	
112	### The finding that matters most for a design tool
113	
114	**The European Accessibility Act never names WCAG.** Searching the full directive text for
115	"WCAG", "Web Content Accessibility", or "EN 301 549" returns nothing. The mechanism is Article
116	15 — conformity is *presumed* for products and services conforming to harmonised standards whose
117	references have been published in the Official Journal:
118	
119	> Products and services which are in conformity with harmonised standards or parts thereof the
120	> references of which have been published in the Official Journal of the European Union, shall be
121	> presumed to be in conformity with the accessibility requirements of this Directive in so far as
122	> those standards or parts thereof cover those requirements.
123	
124	So the chain is EAA → harmonised standard (EN 301 549) → WCAG, and the WCAG version is a
125	property of the standard's edition, not of the law. Any statement of the form "the EAA requires
126	WCAG 2.1 AA" is a two-step inference presented as a citation.
127	
128	## 2. ADA Title II web rule (United States)
129	
130	From ada.gov's own guidance page, verbatim, one sentence carrying three dates:
131	
132	> On April 24, 2024, the Federal Register published the Department of Justice’s (Department)
133	> final rule updating its regulations for Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA).
134	> The final rule has specific requirements about how to ensure that web content and mobile
135	> applications (apps) are accessible to people with disabilities. **On April 20, 2026, the
136	> Federal Register published the Department’s Interim Final Rule (IFR) extending the compliance
137	> date for State and local government entities with a total population of 50,000 or more to
138	> April 26, 2027. The compliance date for public entities with a total population of less than
139	> 50,000, or any special district government, is extended to April 26, 2028.**
140	
141	The technical standard, verbatim:
142	
143	> Requirement: The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) Version **2.1, Level AA** is the
144	> technical standard for state and local governments’ web content and mobile apps.
145	
146	Two scope facts the page states directly. **Title II binds state and local governments, not
147	private businesses** — every example on the page is a city, a state parks department, a town
148	water bill. And a contractor does not escape it: "If a city lets people pay for public parking
149	using a mobile app, that mobile app must meet WCAG 2.1, Level AA even if the app is run by a
150	private company."
151	
152	The page also **names WCAG 3.0 by name** as an example of an acceptable higher standard:
153	
154	> a state parks department would probably be allowed to [use a higher standard] … if that
155	> standard provides the same or more accessibility and usability than WCAG 2.1, Level AA.
156	
157	This confirms the 2.2/3.0 status finding from a second direction: the regulator's own text
158	treats WCAG 3.0 as a hypothetical future alternative, not as anything currently required.
159	
160	**This corrects `accessibility-wcag.md` finding 10, which was at medium confidence and carried
161	reconstructed URLs.** Its dates were right. It is now primary-verified and can be cited.
162	
163	## 3. Section 508 (United States, federal procurement)
164	
165	From the Access Board's Revised 508 Standards, E205.4, verbatim:
166	
167	> Electronic content shall conform to Level A and Level AA Success Criteria and Conformance
168	> Requirements in **WCAG 2.0** (incorporated by reference, see 702.10.1).
169	
170	The software provisions repeat the same bar: "User interface components, as well as the content
171	of platforms and applications, shall conform to Level A and Level AA Success Criteria and
172	Conformance Requirements in WCAG 2.0."
173	
174	There is an exception worth knowing because it is the one place a legal instrument *subtracts*
175	success criteria:
176	
177	> EXCEPTION: Non-Web documents shall not be required to conform to the following four WCAG 2.0
178	> Success Criteria: 2.4.1 Bypass Blocks, 2.4.5 Multiple Ways, 3.2.3 Consistent Navigation, and
179	> 3.2.4 Consistent Identification.
180	
181	### The three-standard spread, verified end to end
182	
183	| Instrument | Named standard | Binds |
184	|---|---|---|
185	| Section 508 (Revised) | **WCAG 2.0** A + AA | US federal ICT procurement |
186	| ADA Title II rule | **WCAG 2.1** AA | US state and local government |
187	| EAA (Directive (EU) 2019/882) | **names no WCAG version at all** | EU products and services in Article 2 scope |
188	
189	**No instrument verified in this pass names WCAG 2.2.** Designing to 2.2 is anticipatory, not
190	compliance — which is the correct reason to do it, since the gap is exactly the six new A/AA
191	criteria and every one of them is cheaper to decide than to retrofit.
192	
193	## 4. Focus management — what the spec actually says, and where it stops
194	
195	WAI-ARIA 1.2, §4.3.1 Information for Authors. This is the closest thing to a normative rule on
196	focus after a destructive DOM change, and it is one sentence:
197	
198	> If the author removes the element with focus, the author SHOULD move focus to a **logical
199	> element**. Similarly, authors SHOULD not scroll the element with focus off screen unless the
200	> user performed a scrolling action.
201	
202	Also normative, and a direct constraint on which ARIA pattern a design may pick:
203	
204	> Authors MUST manage focus on the following container roles: grid, listbox, menu, menubar,
205	> radiogroup, tree, treegrid, tablist
206	
207	And §4.3 on returning to a composite widget:
208	
209	> It is essential that a container maintain a usable and consistent strategy when focus leaves a
210	> container and is then later refocused. While there may be exceptions, it is recommended that
211	> when a previously focused container is refocused, the active descendant be the same element as
212	> the active descendant when the container was last focused. Exceptions include cases where the
213	> contents of a container widget have changed, and widgets like a menubar where the user expects
214	> to always return to the first item when focus leaves the menu bar.
215	
216	**The gap, stated precisely.** A client-side route change is exactly the case the first quote
217	describes — the element with focus is removed — so the obligation to move focus to a logical
218	element does apply. **What the spec does not do is name the destination.** No W3C normative text
219	read in this pass specifies where focus goes on an SPA route change, whether the new page title
220	must be announced, or how the View Transitions API interacts with focus restoration. That is a
221	genuine specification gap, not a lookup failure, and it is why route-change focus has to be a
222	design decision written down rather than a rule to look up.
223	
224	## 5. Live regions — normative, from WAI-ARIA 1.2
225	
226	Definition:
227	
228	> Live regions are perceivable regions of a web page that are typically updated as a result of an
229	> external event **when user focus may be elsewhere**. These regions are not always updated as a
230	> result of a user interaction.
231	
232	The three `aria-live` values, verbatim from §6.7:
233	
234	> **assertive** — Indicates that updates to the region have the highest priority and should be
235	> presented the user immediately.
236	>
237	> **off (default)** — Indicates that updates to the region should not be presented to the user
238	> unless the user is currently focused on that region.
239	>
240	> **polite** — Indicates that updates to the region should be presented at the next graceful
241	> opportunity, such as at the end of speaking the current sentence or when the user pauses typing.
242	
243	The restraint clause is normative, with a SHOULD NOT:
244	
245	> Because an interruption may disorient users or cause them to not complete their current task,
246	> authors **SHOULD NOT use the assertive value unless the interruption is imperative**.
247	
248	And the clause that kills the assumption of deterministic behaviour:
249	
250	> Politeness levels are essentially an ordering mechanism for updates and serve as a **strong
251	> suggestion** to user agents or assistive technologies. The value may be overridden by user
252	> agents, assistive technologies, or the user.
253	
254	Also: `assertive` may *destroy* queued speech — "User agents or assistive technologies MAY choose
255	to clear queued changes when an assertive change occurs."
256	
257	### `role="alert"` vs `role="status"`
258	
259	| | `alert` | `status` |
260	|---|---|---|
261	| Spec description | "A type of live region with important, and usually time-sensitive, information." | "A type of live region whose content is advisory information for the user but is not important enough to justify an alert, often but not necessarily presented as a status bar." |
262	| Implicit `aria-live` | `assertive` | `polite` |
263	| Implicit `aria-atomic` | `true` | `true` |
264	
265	Both quotes and both implicit-value sentences are verbatim from the roles definitions. The
266	`status` role carries one extra normative author obligation:
267	
268	> Authors SHOULD ensure an element with role **status does not receive focus** as a result of
269	> change in status.
270	
271	`alert` additionally: "If the operating system allows, the user agent SHOULD fire a system alert
272	event through the accessibility API when the WAI-ARIA alert is created."
273	
274	Two further live-region roles exist and are rarely used correctly: `log` ("new information is
275	added in meaningful order and old information may disappear") and `marquee` ("non-essential
276	information changes frequently"). `timer` is also a live region role.
277	
278	## 6. Landmarks — from the APG Landmark Regions practice
279	
280	Design-time rules, paraphrased from the page's own bullets:
281	
282	- **One `main` per page**, top-level. Same for `banner` and `contentinfo` — "Each page may have
283	  one contentinfo landmark."
284	- **"A region landmark MUST have a label."** It is the only landmark with a hard label
285	  requirement, and it is the fallback role "used to identify content that named landmarks do not
286	  appropriately describe."
287	- "If a page includes more than one [landmark of a type], each should have a unique label."
288	- The inverse, which nobody encodes: "If a navigation landmark has an identical set of links as
289	  another navigation landmark on the page, **use the same label** for each navigation landmark."
290	- **HTML `header`/`footer` silently stop being landmarks inside `article`, `aside`, `main`,
291	  `nav`, or `section`.** A footer nested in a `section` is not a `contentinfo`. This is a nesting
292	  consequence of a layout decision, invisible on screen.
293	- A `form` landmark "should have a label … visible to all users (e.g. an `h1`-`h6` element)".
294	- Use `search`, not `form`, when the form is a search.
295	
296	**Note for anyone re-running this:** `https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/practices/live-regions/`
297	returns **404**. The APG has seven practice pages (Landmark Regions, Names and Descriptions,
298	Keyboard Interface, Grid and Table Properties, Range-Related Properties, Structural Roles, Hiding
299	Semantics) and **no live-regions practice page exists**. Live-region guidance has to come from
300	the ARIA spec itself, as above.
301	
302	## 7. Accessible names — the five rules, and what an icon-only button owes
303	
304	APG's "Providing Accessible Names and Descriptions" states five rules. The three that are design
305	decisions rather than implementation notes:
306	
307	> **Rule 2: Prefer Visible Text.** In addition to serving as a more robust source for an
308	> accessible name, visible text labels enhance accessibility for many people with disabilities
309	> who do not use assistive technologies that present invisible accessible names. In most
310	> circumstances, visible text labels also make the user interface easier to understand for all
311	> users.
312	
313	> **Rule 4: Avoid Browser Fallback.** … the HTML `title` and `placeholder` attributes are used as
314	> last resort sources of content for accessible names. Because the purpose of these attributes is
315	> not naming, their content typically yields **low quality accessible names that are not
316	> effective**.
317	
318	> **Rule 5: Compose Brief, Useful Names.** Similar to how visually crowded screens and ambiguous
319	> icons reduce usability, excessively long, insufficiently distinct, or unclear accessible names
320	> can make a user interface very difficult, or even impossible, to use for someone who relies on
321	> a non-visual form of the user interface.
322	
323	The `title` attribute specifically:
324	
325	> The `title` attribute is commonly presented visually as a tooltip when the user hovers over the
326	> element with a pointing device, which is **not particularly discoverable, and is also not
327	> accessible to visual users without a pointing device**.
328	
329	**The warning that costs designs content.** Eighteen roles take their name from child content —
330	`button`, `cell`, `checkbox`, `columnheader`, `gridcell`, `heading`, `link`, `menuitem`,
331	`menuitemcheckbox`, `menuitemradio`, `option`, `radio`, `row`, `rowheader`, `switch`, `tab`,
332	`tooltip`, `treeitem` (`menuitem` excludes a child `menu`; `treeitem` excludes a child `group`).
333	On any of them:
334	
335	> If an element with one of the above roles that supports naming from child content is named by
336	> using `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`, content contained in the element and its descendants
337	> is **hidden from assistive technology users** unless the descendant content is referenced by
338	> `aria-labelledby`. It is strongly recommended to avoid using either of these attributes to
339	> override content of one of the above elements except in rare circumstances where hiding content
340	> from assistive technology users is beneficial.
341	
342	And an i18n hook stated on the same page:
343	
344	> When a user interface is translated into multiple languages, ensure that `aria-label` values
345	> are translated.
346	
347	### Icon-only controls — the primary source Task 5 flagged as missing
348	
349	`icons-verified.md` closed with "the accessible name of an icon-only button [was] not checked
350	against a primary source in this pass." It now is. W3C WAI Tutorial, Functional Images:
351	
352	> Functional images are used to initiate actions rather than to convey information. They are used
353	> in buttons, links, and other interactive elements. **The text alternative for the image should
354	> convey the action that will be initiated (the purpose of the image), rather than a description
355	> of the image.**
356	
357	> For instance … the text alternative should be “print this page” rather than “(image of a)
358	> printer”, “search” rather than “magnifying lens” …
359	
360	The failure mode, stated by W3C rather than inferred:
361	
362	> Missing or empty alt values create significant problems for screen reader users because
363	> functional images are essential to the functionality of the content. Screen readers will
364	> typically announce the **image file name, the image URL, or the URL for the link destination**,
365	> which is unlikely to help users understand the action that will be initiated by the image.
366	
367	Worked examples on the page: a stand-alone printer icon takes `alt="Print this page"`; a
368	magnifying-lens search button takes `alt="Search"`; an icon that duplicates adjacent link text
369	takes `alt=""`, "to avoid redundancy and repetition."
370	
371	APG's own canonical case is the same shape: `<button type="button" aria-label="Close">X</button>`.
372	
373	## 8. SC 3.2.6 Consistent Help — the gap `accessibility-wcag.md` finding 11 named
374	
375	That finding established only the Level A designation and said "Treat this as a research gap."
376	Filled here from the Understanding document.
377	
378	What counts as a help mechanism, verbatim:
379	
380	> Typical help mechanisms include: Human contact details such as a phone number, email address,
381	> hours of operation. Human contact mechanism such as a messaging system, chat client, contact
382	> form, social media channel. Self-help option such as an up-to-date Frequently Asked Questions,
383	> How Do I page, Support page. A fully automated contact mechanism such as a chatbot.
384	
385	The requirement is **relative order**, not pixel position:
386	
387	> Regardless of which approach is used, the mechanism must be located in the **same relative
388	> order** on each page within the set of pages.
389	
390	> If the help item is visually in a different location, but in the same serial order, that is not
391	> helpful from a user's point of view, but **it would not fail this criterion**.
392	
393	It does not require help to exist:
394	
395	> It is not the intent of this success criterion to require authors to provide help or access to
396	> help. The Criterion only requires that when one of the listed forms of help is available across
397	> multiple pages that it be in a consistent location.
398	
399	The responsive exception is explicit and narrow:
400	
401	> This exception allows the location in a smaller viewport to be different than in a larger
402	> viewport.
403	
404	…and route navigation does not qualify: "merely navigating between pages within a set of web
405	pages is not a 'change initiated by the user' for the purposes of this exception."
406	
407	Sufficient technique: **G220**, provide a contact-us link in a consistent location. Failure:
408	*Inconsistent Help Location*.
409	
410	## 9. Internationalization
411	
412	### Text expansion — a real table, correctly attributed
413	
414	The W3C i18n article "Text size in translation" republishes IBM's figures. **The number is IBM's,
415	not W3C's**, and the article's own framing is "average expected expansion rates":
416	
417	> The following are average expected expansion rates for text translated from English into
418	> European languages, as published by IBM in their *Guidelines to design global solutions*.
419	
420	| No. of characters in English source | Average expansion |
421	|---|---|
422	| Up to 10 | **200–300%** |
423	| 11–20 | 180–200% |
424	| 21–30 | 160–180% |
425	| 31–50 | 140–160% |
426	| 51–70 | 151–170% |
427	| Over 70 | **130%** |
428	
429	Reproduced exactly as published, including the non-monotonic 51–70 row (151–170%, above the
430	31–50 row's ceiling), which is what the source shows.
431	
432	The load-bearing sentence:
433	
434	> The general message is that text will normally expand, but note carefully how **the smaller the
435	> source message, the higher the likely translation length**.
436	
437	> The problem tends to be that the smaller the English text, the more likely it is to be squeezed
438	> into a small space, such as alongside a form entry field, or inside a graphic, or a set of width
439	> restricted tabs, etc.
440	
441	The article's worked case is the word for "views": one English word, three in Italian
442	(`visualizzazioni`), ratio **3.0**; German `-mal angesehen`, ratio **2.8**. It also names the
443	reverse: Spanish "Idioma de la interfaz" is *shorter* in English, and "smaller translations can
444	be as problematic as bigger ones if they leave too much white space on the page."
445	
446	One measurement rule stated on the page: "Because of the width of the glyphs involved, each
447	Chinese and Korean character is counted as two English characters in width."
448	
449	### CJK line breaking
450	
451	W3C i18n, "Approaches to line breaking". The two parameters that decide everything:
452	
453	> whether 'words' or syllables are separated in the text, and if so, how, and
454	> whether the writing system wraps words, syllables, or characters to the next line.
455	
456	Japanese and Vai wrap **individual characters** "regardless of word or syllable boundaries" —
457	Japanese being mora-based rather than syllable-based, such that text can wrap *inside* a single
458	syllable (きょう). Chinese and Korean wrap syllables, "slightly unusual in that a syllable normally
459	corresponds to a single character, rather than a sequence." South-East Asian scripts including
460	Thai and Khmer have **no word separator at all** and require text analysis to find break points.
461	
462	The rules that are not optional:
463	
464	> It is common to most scripts that content should not start a line with a punctuation mark that
465	> shows the end of a phrase or section.
466	
467	> Other punctuation marks are normally not expected to end a line. These include opening
468	> parentheses or brackets.
469	
470	CSS exposes the Japanese-specific control: the `line-break` property's `strict` and `loose`
471	values decide whether a small kana may be separated from its preceding character — "This can
472	often be useful for text in narrow columns, such as newspapers." An alternative strategy "seen in
473	languages such as Japanese and Chinese involves leaving the punctuation **hanging outside the
474	margin**" — which only works "if there is a visible margin available", i.e. it is a layout
475	decision.
476	
477	### Plural rules — six categories, not two
478	
479	Unicode CLDR, Plural Rules, verbatim:
480	
481	> Languages vary in how they handle plurals of nouns or unit expressions (“hour” vs “hours”, and
482	> so on). Some languages have two forms, like English; some languages have only a single form; and
483	> some languages have multiple forms. CLDR uses short, mnemonic tags for these plural categories:
484	
485	`zero` · `one` (singular) · `two` (dual) · `few` (paucal) · `many` (also used for fractions if
486	they have a separate class) · `other` (required — general plural form — also used if the language
487	only has a single form).
488	
489	The categories are **not grammatical categories**:
490	
491	> The CLDR plural categories do not necessarily match the traditional grammatical categories.
492	> Instead, the categories are determined by changes required in a phrase or sentence if a numeric
493	> placeholder changes value.
494	
495	CLDR's own worked example shows `few` covering 2–4, 22–24, 32–34 while `other` covers 0, 5–20,
496	25–30 — so the mapping from number to category is not a range check either. And the stated reason
497	the whole mechanism exists is a design one: it allows "more natural phrasing than constructions
498	like '1 hour(s)'."
499	
500	---
501	
502	## Not established in this pass — verify before relying on any of it
503	
504	Named explicitly so silence is not read as agreement.
505	
506	- **EN 301 549's current version and its WCAG edition.** ETSI was not fetched. The claim in
507	  `accessibility-wcag.md` that v3.2.1 incorporates WCAG 2.1 and that v4.1.1 moves to WCAG 2.2 AA
508	  with an OJEU citation "anticipated around October 2026" remains at that file's *medium*
509	  confidence and is **forward-looking**. Do not state a version number or an OJEU date.
510	- **Whether any EU member state's transposition names a WCAG version directly.** Transposition is
511	  national and 27-way; none was read.
512	- **Whether the EAA reaches non-EU companies selling into the EU.** The directive's territorial
513	  scope was not analysed and no quote supports either answer.
514	- **ADA Title III (private business) obligations.** The rule read here is Title II only. There is
515	  no equivalent DOJ web regulation for Title III verified in this pass; anything about private-
516	  sector ADA web liability is litigation history, not a named standard, and was not researched.
517	- **Where focus should go on an SPA route change.** Confirmed above as a specification gap. The
518	  common practitioner answers — a `tabindex="-1"` heading, the `main` landmark, a skip link, a
519	  visually-hidden route announcer — are not in any W3C normative text read here.
520	- **The View Transitions API's interaction with focus and `prefers-reduced-motion`.** Not read.
521	- **"A live region must exist in the DOM before content is injected into it."** This is very
522	  widely repeated and it is **not in the WAI-ARIA 1.2 text read in this pass**. It may be true of
523	  specific screen-reader implementations. It is not a spec requirement as far as this pass
524	  established.
525	- **Cross-screen-reader live-region behaviour** (NVDA / JAWS / VoiceOver differences, `aria-atomic`
526	  and `aria-relevant` support levels). No support table was fetched. The spec's own "strong
527	  suggestion … may be overridden" clause is the only verified statement about variability.
528	- **A measured figure for the cost of icon-only controls.** W3C states functional-image alt text
529	  as a requirement; no comprehension study, error rate, or task-time measurement was located.
530	  `icons-verified.md` already flags this and it is still open.
531	- **Any specific text-expansion percentage other than IBM's table above.** If a run needs a number
532	  for a language not covered by "European languages", it does not have one.
533	- **RTL mirroring rules beyond `§13`'s existing statement.** Not researched here.
534	
535	## What goes where
536	
537	| Finding | File |
538	|---|---|
539	| EAA dates, scope, microenterprise threshold, the WCAG-is-absent finding | `ACCESS.md` legal section |
540	| Title II standard + April 2027 / April 2028 compliance dates | `ACCESS.md` legal section |
541	| Section 508 → WCAG 2.0; the three-standard spread table | `ACCESS.md` legal section |
542	| ARIA §4.3.1 focus-on-removal SHOULD; the MUST-manage-focus role list | `ACCESS.md` focus section |
543	| SPA route-change destination as a named specification gap | `ACCESS.md` focus section |
544	| `aria-live` values, the assertive SHOULD NOT, alert vs status table | `ACCESS.md` live regions |
545	| Landmark rules; `header`/`footer` nesting trap; region MUST have a label | `ACCESS.md` structure |
546	| Five naming rules; the name-from-content hiding warning | `ACCESS.md` accessible names |
547	| Functional-image alt: name the action, not the picture | `ACCESS.md`, `CRAFT.md` icons |
548	| SC 3.2.6 relative-order requirement and its responsive exception | `ACCESS.md` WCAG 2.2 section |
549	| IBM expansion table; CJK wrapping; CLDR six plural categories | `ACCESS.md` i18n section |

# Verified — legal enforcement, focus management, live regions, accessible names, i18n

**Date:** 2026-08-02
**Method:** rendered DOM text pulled with a headless browser from the primary source itself,
then read in context. **Not** WebFetch summaries and **not** from memory. This project has
already caught four instances of plausible-but-wrong content, including one claim that
contradicted its own cited source, so every quote below was read off the live rendered page.
`curl` is useless for most of these: EUR-Lex and the W3C TR pages are JS-rendered and return a
near-empty shell to a plain fetch.

**Why this pass exists.** Two areas returned **zero surviving claims across three separate
research-workflow attempts**: legal enforcement (`accessibility-wcag.md` finding 10 at *medium*
confidence and explicitly flagged "MUST be re-verified against the primary texts";
`native-a11y-verified.md` HALF TWO, zero claims) and SPA focus management / live regions
(`web-a11y-patterns.md` finding 8, zero claims). Law and spec sites defeat summarizers. The
browser is what works.

**The rule this file is written under:** a wrong compliance deadline in a design tool is worse
than an absent one, because someone could rely on it. Everything not verified below is named
in the final section as *not established in this pass*, and nothing there ships as fact.

Pages read:

| Source | URL |
|---|---|
| Directive (EU) 2019/882 — European Accessibility Act | `https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32019L0882` |
| DOJ — ADA Title II web rule guidance | `https://www.ada.gov/resources/2024-03-08-web-rule/` |
| US Access Board — Revised Section 508 Standards (ICT) | `https://www.access-board.gov/ict/` |
| WAI-ARIA 1.2 (Recommendation) | `https://www.w3.org/TR/wai-aria-1.2/` |
| ARIA APG — Landmark Regions | `https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/practices/landmark-regions/` |
| ARIA APG — Providing Accessible Names and Descriptions | `https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/practices/names-and-descriptions/` |
| WAI Tutorial — Functional Images | `https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/images/functional/` |
| Understanding SC 3.2.6 Consistent Help | `https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/consistent-help.html` |
| W3C i18n — Text size in translation | `https://www.w3.org/International/articles/article-text-size` |
| W3C i18n — Approaches to line breaking | `https://www.w3.org/International/articles/typography/linebreak.en` |
| Unicode CLDR — Plural Rules | `https://cldr.unicode.org/index/cldr-spec/plural-rules` |

The ADA page carries a dateline of **April 08, 2024** with the April 2026 extension folded into
its opening paragraph. EUR-Lex serves the consolidated directive text. W3C pages carry a 2026
copyright line.

---

## 1. The European Accessibility Act — Directive (EU) 2019/882

### The dates, verbatim from Article 31

> 1.   Member States shall adopt and publish, by 28 June 2022, the laws, regulations and
> administrative provisions necessary to comply with this Directive. They shall immediately
> communicate the text of those measures to the Commission.
>
> 2.   They shall apply those measures from **28 June 2025**.
>
> 3.   By way of derogation from paragraph 2 of this Article, Member States may decide to apply
> the measures regarding the obligations set out in Article 4(8) at the latest from 28 June 2027.

Article 2 scopes the same date to the goods and services themselves — products "placed on the
market **after 28 June 2025**", services "provided to consumers **after 28 June 2025**".

**Article 32 is the part almost every summary drops.** There is a long transitional tail:

> Member States shall provide for a transitional period ending on **28 June 2030** during which
> service providers may continue to provide their services using products which were lawfully
> used by them to provide similar services before that date.
>
> Service contracts agreed before 28 June 2025 may continue without alteration until they
> expire, but no longer than **five years** from that date.

Self-service terminals lawfully in use before 28 June 2025 may run "until the end of their
economically useful life, but no longer than **20 years** after their entry into use."

So "the EAA applied from 28 June 2025" is true and incomplete: legacy content and legacy
hardware have their own clocks running to 2030 and beyond.

### What is actually in scope

Products (Article 2(1)): consumer general-purpose computer hardware systems and their operating
systems; payment terminals; ATMs, ticketing machines, check-in machines and interactive
self-service information terminals; consumer terminal equipment with interactive computing
capability used for electronic communications services; the same for accessing audiovisual media
services; and e-readers.

Services (Article 2(2)): electronic communications services; services providing access to
audiovisual media services; named elements of air, bus, rail and waterborne passenger transport
(websites, mobile apps, e-tickets, travel information, interactive self-service terminals);
**consumer banking services**; **e-books and dedicated software**; and **e-commerce services**.
Article 2(3) adds answering emergency communications to 112.

Content exempted from the website/app obligations includes "pre-recorded time-based media
published before 28 June 2025", "office file formats published before 28 June 2025", and
archives containing only content not updated or edited after 28 June 2025.

### The microenterprise exemption, with its actual threshold

Article 3 definition, verbatim:

> ‘microenterprise’ means an enterprise which employs **fewer than 10 persons** and which has an
> annual turnover **not exceeding EUR 2 million** or an annual balance sheet total not exceeding
> EUR 2 million;

Article 4(5), verbatim:

> Microenterprises providing services shall be exempt from complying with the accessibility
> requirements referred to in paragraph 3 of this Article and any obligations relating to the
> compliance with those requirements.

Note the asymmetry, which is stated in Recital: microenterprises **providing services** are
exempt outright; microenterprises **dealing with products** are not exempt — their obligations
are merely "lighter", and Article 14(4) exempts them only from *documenting* their
disproportionate-burden assessment, not from making it.

### The finding that matters most for a design tool

**The European Accessibility Act never names WCAG.** Searching the full directive text for
"WCAG", "Web Content Accessibility", or "EN 301 549" returns nothing. The mechanism is Article
15 — conformity is *presumed* for products and services conforming to harmonised standards whose
references have been published in the Official Journal:

> Products and services which are in conformity with harmonised standards or parts thereof the
> references of which have been published in the Official Journal of the European Union, shall be
> presumed to be in conformity with the accessibility requirements of this Directive in so far as
> those standards or parts thereof cover those requirements.

So the chain is EAA → harmonised standard (EN 301 549) → WCAG, and the WCAG version is a
property of the standard's edition, not of the law. Any statement of the form "the EAA requires
WCAG 2.1 AA" is a two-step inference presented as a citation.

## 2. ADA Title II web rule (United States)

From ada.gov's own guidance page, verbatim, one sentence carrying three dates:

> On April 24, 2024, the Federal Register published the Department of Justice’s (Department)
> final rule updating its regulations for Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA).
> The final rule has specific requirements about how to ensure that web content and mobile
> applications (apps) are accessible to people with disabilities. **On April 20, 2026, the
> Federal Register published the Department’s Interim Final Rule (IFR) extending the compliance
> date for State and local government entities with a total population of 50,000 or more to
> April 26, 2027. The compliance date for public entities with a total population of less than
> 50,000, or any special district government, is extended to April 26, 2028.**

The technical standard, verbatim:

> Requirement: The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) Version **2.1, Level AA** is the
> technical standard for state and local governments’ web content and mobile apps.

Two scope facts the page states directly. **Title II binds state and local governments, not
private businesses** — every example on the page is a city, a state parks department, a town
water bill. And a contractor does not escape it: "If a city lets people pay for public parking
using a mobile app, that mobile app must meet WCAG 2.1, Level AA even if the app is run by a
private company."

The page also **names WCAG 3.0 by name** as an example of an acceptable higher standard:

> a state parks department would probably be allowed to [use a higher standard] … if that
> standard provides the same or more accessibility and usability than WCAG 2.1, Level AA.

This confirms the 2.2/3.0 status finding from a second direction: the regulator's own text
treats WCAG 3.0 as a hypothetical future alternative, not as anything currently required.

**This corrects `accessibility-wcag.md` finding 10, which was at medium confidence and carried
reconstructed URLs.** Its dates were right. It is now primary-verified and can be cited.

## 3. Section 508 (United States, federal procurement)

From the Access Board's Revised 508 Standards, E205.4, verbatim:

> Electronic content shall conform to Level A and Level AA Success Criteria and Conformance
> Requirements in **WCAG 2.0** (incorporated by reference, see 702.10.1).

The software provisions repeat the same bar: "User interface components, as well as the content
of platforms and applications, shall conform to Level A and Level AA Success Criteria and
Conformance Requirements in WCAG 2.0."

There is an exception worth knowing because it is the one place a legal instrument *subtracts*
success criteria:

> EXCEPTION: Non-Web documents shall not be required to conform to the following four WCAG 2.0
> Success Criteria: 2.4.1 Bypass Blocks, 2.4.5 Multiple Ways, 3.2.3 Consistent Navigation, and
> 3.2.4 Consistent Identification.

### The three-standard spread, verified end to end

| Instrument | Named standard | Binds |
|---|---|---|
| Section 508 (Revised) | **WCAG 2.0** A + AA | US federal ICT procurement |
| ADA Title II rule | **WCAG 2.1** AA | US state and local government |
| EAA (Directive (EU) 2019/882) | **names no WCAG version at all** | EU products and services in Article 2 scope |

**No instrument verified in this pass names WCAG 2.2.** Designing to 2.2 is anticipatory, not
compliance — which is the correct reason to do it, since the gap is exactly the six new A/AA
criteria and every one of them is cheaper to decide than to retrofit.

## 4. Focus management — what the spec actually says, and where it stops

WAI-ARIA 1.2, §4.3.1 Information for Authors. This is the closest thing to a normative rule on
focus after a destructive DOM change, and it is one sentence:

> If the author removes the element with focus, the author SHOULD move focus to a **logical
> element**. Similarly, authors SHOULD not scroll the element with focus off screen unless the
> user performed a scrolling action.

Also normative, and a direct constraint on which ARIA pattern a design may pick:

> Authors MUST manage focus on the following container roles: grid, listbox, menu, menubar,
> radiogroup, tree, treegrid, tablist

And §4.3 on returning to a composite widget:

> It is essential that a container maintain a usable and consistent strategy when focus leaves a
> container and is then later refocused. While there may be exceptions, it is recommended that
> when a previously focused container is refocused, the active descendant be the same element as
> the active descendant when the container was last focused. Exceptions include cases where the
> contents of a container widget have changed, and widgets like a menubar where the user expects
> to always return to the first item when focus leaves the menu bar.

**The gap, stated precisely.** A client-side route change is exactly the case the first quote
describes — the element with focus is removed — so the obligation to move focus to a logical
element does apply. **What the spec does not do is name the destination.** No W3C normative text
read in this pass specifies where focus goes on an SPA route change, whether the new page title
must be announced, or how the View Transitions API interacts with focus restoration. That is a
genuine specification gap, not a lookup failure, and it is why route-change focus has to be a
design decision written down rather than a rule to look up.

## 5. Live regions — normative, from WAI-ARIA 1.2

Definition:

> Live regions are perceivable regions of a web page that are typically updated as a result of an
> external event **when user focus may be elsewhere**. These regions are not always updated as a
> result of a user interaction.

The three `aria-live` values, verbatim from §6.7:

> **assertive** — Indicates that updates to the region have the highest priority and should be
> presented the user immediately.
>
> **off (default)** — Indicates that updates to the region should not be presented to the user
> unless the user is currently focused on that region.
>
> **polite** — Indicates that updates to the region should be presented at the next graceful
> opportunity, such as at the end of speaking the current sentence or when the user pauses typing.

The restraint clause is normative, with a SHOULD NOT:

> Because an interruption may disorient users or cause them to not complete their current task,
> authors **SHOULD NOT use the assertive value unless the interruption is imperative**.

And the clause that kills the assumption of deterministic behaviour:

> Politeness levels are essentially an ordering mechanism for updates and serve as a **strong
> suggestion** to user agents or assistive technologies. The value may be overridden by user
> agents, assistive technologies, or the user.

Also: `assertive` may *destroy* queued speech — "User agents or assistive technologies MAY choose
to clear queued changes when an assertive change occurs."

### `role="alert"` vs `role="status"`

| | `alert` | `status` |
|---|---|---|
| Spec description | "A type of live region with important, and usually time-sensitive, information." | "A type of live region whose content is advisory information for the user but is not important enough to justify an alert, often but not necessarily presented as a status bar." |
| Implicit `aria-live` | `assertive` | `polite` |
| Implicit `aria-atomic` | `true` | `true` |

Both quotes and both implicit-value sentences are verbatim from the roles definitions. The
`status` role carries one extra normative author obligation:

> Authors SHOULD ensure an element with role **status does not receive focus** as a result of
> change in status.

`alert` additionally: "If the operating system allows, the user agent SHOULD fire a system alert
event through the accessibility API when the WAI-ARIA alert is created."

Two further live-region roles exist and are rarely used correctly: `log` ("new information is
added in meaningful order and old information may disappear") and `marquee` ("non-essential
information changes frequently"). `timer` is also a live region role.

## 6. Landmarks — from the APG Landmark Regions practice

Design-time rules, paraphrased from the page's own bullets:

- **One `main` per page**, top-level. Same for `banner` and `contentinfo` — "Each page may have
  one contentinfo landmark."
- **"A region landmark MUST have a label."** It is the only landmark with a hard label
  requirement, and it is the fallback role "used to identify content that named landmarks do not
  appropriately describe."
- "If a page includes more than one [landmark of a type], each should have a unique label."
- The inverse, which nobody encodes: "If a navigation landmark has an identical set of links as
  another navigation landmark on the page, **use the same label** for each navigation landmark."
- **HTML `header`/`footer` silently stop being landmarks inside `article`, `aside`, `main`,
  `nav`, or `section`.** A footer nested in a `section` is not a `contentinfo`. This is a nesting
  consequence of a layout decision, invisible on screen.
- A `form` landmark "should have a label … visible to all users (e.g. an `h1`-`h6` element)".
- Use `search`, not `form`, when the form is a search.

**Note for anyone re-running this:** `https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/practices/live-regions/`
returns **404**. The APG has seven practice pages (Landmark Regions, Names and Descriptions,
Keyboard Interface, Grid and Table Properties, Range-Related Properties, Structural Roles, Hiding
Semantics) and **no live-regions practice page exists**. Live-region guidance has to come from
the ARIA spec itself, as above.

## 7. Accessible names — the five rules, and what an icon-only button owes

APG's "Providing Accessible Names and Descriptions" states five rules. The three that are design
decisions rather than implementation notes:

> **Rule 2: Prefer Visible Text.** In addition to serving as a more robust source for an
> accessible name, visible text labels enhance accessibility for many people with disabilities
> who do not use assistive technologies that present invisible accessible names. In most
> circumstances, visible text labels also make the user interface easier to understand for all
> users.

> **Rule 4: Avoid Browser Fallback.** … the HTML `title` and `placeholder` attributes are used as
> last resort sources of content for accessible names. Because the purpose of these attributes is
> not naming, their content typically yields **low quality accessible names that are not
> effective**.

> **Rule 5: Compose Brief, Useful Names.** Similar to how visually crowded screens and ambiguous
> icons reduce usability, excessively long, insufficiently distinct, or unclear accessible names
> can make a user interface very difficult, or even impossible, to use for someone who relies on
> a non-visual form of the user interface.

The `title` attribute specifically:

> The `title` attribute is commonly presented visually as a tooltip when the user hovers over the
> element with a pointing device, which is **not particularly discoverable, and is also not
> accessible to visual users without a pointing device**.

**The warning that costs designs content.** Eighteen roles take their name from child content —
`button`, `cell`, `checkbox`, `columnheader`, `gridcell`, `heading`, `link`, `menuitem`,
`menuitemcheckbox`, `menuitemradio`, `option`, `radio`, `row`, `rowheader`, `switch`, `tab`,
`tooltip`, `treeitem` (`menuitem` excludes a child `menu`; `treeitem` excludes a child `group`).
On any of them:

> If an element with one of the above roles that supports naming from child content is named by
> using `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`, content contained in the element and its descendants
> is **hidden from assistive technology users** unless the descendant content is referenced by
> `aria-labelledby`. It is strongly recommended to avoid using either of these attributes to
> override content of one of the above elements except in rare circumstances where hiding content
> from assistive technology users is beneficial.

And an i18n hook stated on the same page:

> When a user interface is translated into multiple languages, ensure that `aria-label` values
> are translated.

### Icon-only controls — the primary source Task 5 flagged as missing

`icons-verified.md` closed with "the accessible name of an icon-only button [was] not checked
against a primary source in this pass." It now is. W3C WAI Tutorial, Functional Images:

> Functional images are used to initiate actions rather than to convey information. They are used
> in buttons, links, and other interactive elements. **The text alternative for the image should
> convey the action that will be initiated (the purpose of the image), rather than a description
> of the image.**

> For instance … the text alternative should be “print this page” rather than “(image of a)
> printer”, “search” rather than “magnifying lens” …

The failure mode, stated by W3C rather than inferred:

> Missing or empty alt values create significant problems for screen reader users because
> functional images are essential to the functionality of the content. Screen readers will
> typically announce the **image file name, the image URL, or the URL for the link destination**,
> which is unlikely to help users understand the action that will be initiated by the image.

Worked examples on the page: a stand-alone printer icon takes `alt="Print this page"`; a
magnifying-lens search button takes `alt="Search"`; an icon that duplicates adjacent link text
takes `alt=""`, "to avoid redundancy and repetition."

APG's own canonical case is the same shape: `<button type="button" aria-label="Close">X</button>`.

## 8. SC 3.2.6 Consistent Help — the gap `accessibility-wcag.md` finding 11 named

That finding established only the Level A designation and said "Treat this as a research gap."
Filled here from the Understanding document.

What counts as a help mechanism, verbatim:

> Typical help mechanisms include: Human contact details such as a phone number, email address,
> hours of operation. Human contact mechanism such as a messaging system, chat client, contact
> form, social media channel. Self-help option such as an up-to-date Frequently Asked Questions,
> How Do I page, Support page. A fully automated contact mechanism such as a chatbot.

The requirement is **relative order**, not pixel position:

> Regardless of which approach is used, the mechanism must be located in the **same relative
> order** on each page within the set of pages.

> If the help item is visually in a different location, but in the same serial order, that is not
> helpful from a user's point of view, but **it would not fail this criterion**.

It does not require help to exist:

> It is not the intent of this success criterion to require authors to provide help or access to
> help. The Criterion only requires that when one of the listed forms of help is available across
> multiple pages that it be in a consistent location.

The responsive exception is explicit and narrow:

> This exception allows the location in a smaller viewport to be different than in a larger
> viewport.

…and route navigation does not qualify: "merely navigating between pages within a set of web
pages is not a 'change initiated by the user' for the purposes of this exception."

Sufficient technique: **G220**, provide a contact-us link in a consistent location. Failure:
*Inconsistent Help Location*.

## 9. Internationalization

### Text expansion — a real table, correctly attributed

The W3C i18n article "Text size in translation" republishes IBM's figures. **The number is IBM's,
not W3C's**, and the article's own framing is "average expected expansion rates":

> The following are average expected expansion rates for text translated from English into
> European languages, as published by IBM in their *Guidelines to design global solutions*.

| No. of characters in English source | Average expansion |
|---|---|
| Up to 10 | **200–300%** |
| 11–20 | 180–200% |
| 21–30 | 160–180% |
| 31–50 | 140–160% |
| 51–70 | 151–170% |
| Over 70 | **130%** |

Reproduced exactly as published, including the non-monotonic 51–70 row (151–170%, above the
31–50 row's ceiling), which is what the source shows.

The load-bearing sentence:

> The general message is that text will normally expand, but note carefully how **the smaller the
> source message, the higher the likely translation length**.

> The problem tends to be that the smaller the English text, the more likely it is to be squeezed
> into a small space, such as alongside a form entry field, or inside a graphic, or a set of width
> restricted tabs, etc.

The article's worked case is the word for "views": one English word, three in Italian
(`visualizzazioni`), ratio **3.0**; German `-mal angesehen`, ratio **2.8**. It also names the
reverse: Spanish "Idioma de la interfaz" is *shorter* in English, and "smaller translations can
be as problematic as bigger ones if they leave too much white space on the page."

One measurement rule stated on the page: "Because of the width of the glyphs involved, each
Chinese and Korean character is counted as two English characters in width."

### CJK line breaking

W3C i18n, "Approaches to line breaking". The two parameters that decide everything:

> whether 'words' or syllables are separated in the text, and if so, how, and
> whether the writing system wraps words, syllables, or characters to the next line.

Japanese and Vai wrap **individual characters** "regardless of word or syllable boundaries" —
Japanese being mora-based rather than syllable-based, such that text can wrap *inside* a single
syllable (きょう). Chinese and Korean wrap syllables, "slightly unusual in that a syllable normally
corresponds to a single character, rather than a sequence." South-East Asian scripts including
Thai and Khmer have **no word separator at all** and require text analysis to find break points.

The rules that are not optional:

> It is common to most scripts that content should not start a line with a punctuation mark that
> shows the end of a phrase or section.

> Other punctuation marks are normally not expected to end a line. These include opening
> parentheses or brackets.

CSS exposes the Japanese-specific control: the `line-break` property's `strict` and `loose`
values decide whether a small kana may be separated from its preceding character — "This can
often be useful for text in narrow columns, such as newspapers." An alternative strategy "seen in
languages such as Japanese and Chinese involves leaving the punctuation **hanging outside the
margin**" — which only works "if there is a visible margin available", i.e. it is a layout
decision.

### Plural rules — six categories, not two

Unicode CLDR, Plural Rules, verbatim:

> Languages vary in how they handle plurals of nouns or unit expressions (“hour” vs “hours”, and
> so on). Some languages have two forms, like English; some languages have only a single form; and
> some languages have multiple forms. CLDR uses short, mnemonic tags for these plural categories:

`zero` · `one` (singular) · `two` (dual) · `few` (paucal) · `many` (also used for fractions if
they have a separate class) · `other` (required — general plural form — also used if the language
only has a single form).

The categories are **not grammatical categories**:

> The CLDR plural categories do not necessarily match the traditional grammatical categories.
> Instead, the categories are determined by changes required in a phrase or sentence if a numeric
> placeholder changes value.

CLDR's own worked example shows `few` covering 2–4, 22–24, 32–34 while `other` covers 0, 5–20,
25–30 — so the mapping from number to category is not a range check either. And the stated reason
the whole mechanism exists is a design one: it allows "more natural phrasing than constructions
like '1 hour(s)'."

---

## Not established in this pass — verify before relying on any of it

Named explicitly so silence is not read as agreement.

- **EN 301 549's current version and its WCAG edition.** ETSI was not fetched. The claim in
  `accessibility-wcag.md` that v3.2.1 incorporates WCAG 2.1 and that v4.1.1 moves to WCAG 2.2 AA
  with an OJEU citation "anticipated around October 2026" remains at that file's *medium*
  confidence and is **forward-looking**. Do not state a version number or an OJEU date.
- **Whether any EU member state's transposition names a WCAG version directly.** Transposition is
  national and 27-way; none was read.
- **Whether the EAA reaches non-EU companies selling into the EU.** The directive's territorial
  scope was not analysed and no quote supports either answer.
- **ADA Title III (private business) obligations.** The rule read here is Title II only. There is
  no equivalent DOJ web regulation for Title III verified in this pass; anything about private-
  sector ADA web liability is litigation history, not a named standard, and was not researched.
- **Where focus should go on an SPA route change.** Confirmed above as a specification gap. The
  common practitioner answers — a `tabindex="-1"` heading, the `main` landmark, a skip link, a
  visually-hidden route announcer — are not in any W3C normative text read here.
- **The View Transitions API's interaction with focus and `prefers-reduced-motion`.** Not read.
- **"A live region must exist in the DOM before content is injected into it."** This is very
  widely repeated and it is **not in the WAI-ARIA 1.2 text read in this pass**. It may be true of
  specific screen-reader implementations. It is not a spec requirement as far as this pass
  established.
- **Cross-screen-reader live-region behaviour** (NVDA / JAWS / VoiceOver differences, `aria-atomic`
  and `aria-relevant` support levels). No support table was fetched. The spec's own "strong
  suggestion … may be overridden" clause is the only verified statement about variability.
- **A measured figure for the cost of icon-only controls.** W3C states functional-image alt text
  as a requirement; no comprehension study, error rate, or task-time measurement was located.
  `icons-verified.md` already flags this and it is still open.
- **Any specific text-expansion percentage other than IBM's table above.** If a run needs a number
  for a language not covered by "European languages", it does not have one.
- **RTL mirroring rules beyond `§13`'s existing statement.** Not researched here.

144-When encountering this navigation region, a screen reader user will hear the name and role of the element, e.g., "Product navigation region", and then be able to read through the links contained in the region. 145-Warning 146:If aria-label is applied to an element with one of the roles that supports naming from child content, content contained in the element and its descendants is hidden from assistive technology users. 147-It is strongly recommended to avoid using aria-label to override content of one of these elements except in rare circumstances where hiding content from assistive technology users is beneficial. 148-There are certain types of elements, such as paragraphs and list items, that should not be named with aria-label. 149-They are identified in the table in the Accessible Name Guidance by Role section. 150-Because the value of aria-label is not rendered visually, testing with assistive technologies to ensure the expected name is presented to users is particularly important. 151-When a user interface is translated into multiple languages, ensure that aria-label values are translated. 152-Naming with Referenced Content Via aria-labelledby 153-The aria-labelledby property enables authors to reference other elements on the page to define an accessible name. 154-For example, the following switch is named by the text content of a previous sibling element. 155-Night mode 156- 157-Note that while using aria-labelledby is similar in this situation to using an HTML label element with the for attribute, one significant difference is that browsers do not automatically make clicking on the labeling element activate the labeled element; that is an author responsibility. 158-However, HTML label cannot be used to label a span element. 159-Fortunately, an HTML input with type="checkbox" allows the ARIA switch role, so when feasible, using the following approach creates a more robust solution. 160- 161- 162-The aria-labelledby property is useful in a wide variety of situations because: 163-It has the highest precedence when browsers calculate accessible names, i.e., it overrides names from child content and all other naming attributes, including aria-label. 164-It can concatenate content from multiple elements into a single name string. 165-It incorporates content from elements regardless of their visibility, i.e., it even includes content from elements with the HTML hidden attribute, CSS display: none, or CSS visibility: hidden in the calculated name string. 166-It incorporates the value of input elements, i.e., if it references a textbox, the value of the textbox is included in the calculated name string. 167-An example of referencing a hidden element with aria-labelledby could be a label for a night switch control: 168-Night mode 169- 170-In some cases, the most effective name for an element is its own content combined with the content of another element. 171-Because aria-labelledby has highest precedence in name calculation, in those situations, it is possible to use aria-labelledby to reference both the element itself and the other element. 172-In the following example, the "Read more..." link is named by the element itself and the article’s heading, resulting in a name for the link of "Read more... 7 ways you can help save the bees". 173-

7 ways you can help save the bees

174-

Bees are disappearing rapidly. Here are seven things you can do to help.

175-

Read more...

176-When multiple elements are referenced by aria-labelledby, text content from each referenced element is concatenated in the order specified in the aria-labelledby value. -- 187:If aria-labelledby is applied to an element with one of the roles that supports naming from child content, content contained in the element and its descendants is hidden from assistive technology users unless it is also referenced by aria-labelledby. 188-It is strongly recommended to avoid using this attribute to override content of one of these elements except in rare circumstances where hiding content from assistive technology users is beneficial. 189-Because calculating the name of an element with aria-labelledby can be complex and reference hidden content, testing with assistive technologies to ensure the expected name is presented to users is particularly important. 190-Naming Form Controls with the Label Element 191-The HTML label element enables authors to identify content that serves as a label and associate it with a form control. 192-When a label element is associated with a form control, browsers calculate an accessible name for the form control from the label content. 193-For example, text displayed adjacent to a checkbox may be visually associated with the checkbox, so it is understood as the checkbox label by users who can perceive that visual association. 194-However, unless the text is programmatically associated with the checkbox, assistive technology users will experience a checkbox without a label. 195-HTML provides two ways of associating a label with a form control. 196-The one that provides the broadest browser and assistive technology support is to set the for attribute on the label element to the id of the control. 197-This way of associating the label with the control is often called explicit association.

content.text:
Verification complete. Both primary sources checked live, all mechanical checks run.

---

# Task 8 Review — `ACCESS.md` + `legal-and-focus-verified.md`

## Spec compliance: ✅

Every brief item landed. Structural claim opens the file. Page-shaped/tool-shaped fork present (and `check.sh` now passes it — one failure cleared, none added). Six WCAG 2.2 A/AA criteria as design decisions. ARIA-as-keyboard-model. WebAIM restraint case. Native divergence. i18n folded in, not split out. Legal from Step 1 research. Diff is exactly two new files, nothing else touched.

---

## THE PRIORITY CHECK — both claims **CONFIRMED**

### Claim 1: "The EAA never names WCAG at all" — **correct, and it contradicts the commentary**

I pulled the full consolidated Directive (EU) 2019/882 from EUR-Lex. Confirmed the fetch was complete, not a shell: `Whereas:` recitals present, Articles 1–33 present, `ANNEX I` through `ANNEX VI` all present.

```
grep -ic "WCAG"                     → 0
grep -i  "Web Content Accessibility" → 0
grep -i  "W3C"                       → 0
grep -i  "301 549" / "ETSI"          → 0
```

Article 15 ("Presumption of conformity") reads exactly as `ACCESS.md` quotes it — conformity is *presumed* for products and services conforming to harmonised standards whose references are published in the OJEU. `ACCESS.md:1224`'s conclusion is right: **"Any sentence of the form 'the EAA requires WCAG 2.1 AA' is a two-step inference presented as a citation."** Confirming this is worth the pass — it is the opposite of what most secondary commentary says.

One detail that raises my confidence in the implementer's judgment rather than lowering it: `legal-and-focus-verified.md:124` writes the chain as "EAA → harmonised standard **(EN 301 549)** → WCAG". That parenthetical is itself an unverified inference — the directive never names EN 301 549. **`ACCESS.md:1223` dropped it.** The shipped file is more conservative than its own research doc. That is the correct direction for a leak to run.

### Claim 2: DOJ April 2026 extension — **correct, verbatim**

ada.gov returns the exact sentence `ACCESS.md:1231-1237` quotes:

> On April 20, 2026, the Federal Register published the Department's Interim Final Rule (IFR) extending the compliance date for State and local government entities with a total population of 50,000 or more to **April 26, 2027**. The compliance date for public entities with a total population of less than 50,000, or any special district government, is extended to **April 26, 2028**.

Also confirmed on the same page: WCAG 2.1 Level AA as the technical standard; the parking-app contractor example verbatim; DOJ naming WCAG 3.0 as a hypothetical acceptable higher standard.

---

## Honesty of the unverified list — **confirmed, all three**

| Claimed unestablished | Grep result in `ACCESS.md` |
|---|---|
| EN 301 549 edition | `301 549\|ETSI\|v3.2.1\|v4.1.1` → **only** lines 1262 and 1342, both "not established in this pass". §12's chain stops at "harmonised standard" and does not complete to a WCAG version. Zero confident assertions. |
| Cross-screen-reader live-region behaviour | `NVDA\|JAWS` → **only** lines 759 and 1337, both disclaimers. The other six `VoiceOver` hits are Apple-native grouping/label/alt-text claims, none about live regions. "Must exist in the DOM before injection" appears **only as a negation** (757, 1335). |
| SPA route-change focus | §6 names it a specification gap, requires the decision, supplies no destination. **More conservative than the report describes** — the practitioner answers (`tabindex="-1"` heading, `main`, skip link, route announcer) stayed in the research doc and were not carried into the shipped file at all. |

No leak in any of the three. One unrelated leak found — see Minor 1.

---

## Everything else verified

- **Six new A/AA criteria** all present as decisions: 2.5.8, 2.5.7, 2.4.11, 3.3.8, 3.3.7, 3.2.6.
- **2.5.8 spacing geometry** (`SURFACES.md:161` defers, `ACCESS.md:119-142` delivers): 24 px circle, no-intersection rule, plus three consequences (24 px centre-to-centre, diagonal failure, neighbour's box not its circle) — each labeled as derivation, not quotation. Correct handling.
- **17 pt contrast boundary** — `SURFACES.md:284-286` hands off, `ACCESS.md` §3 carries the full Apple table with the "iOS body is 17 pt, on the strict side" consequence. ✅
- **Reduce Transparency / Increase Contrast** — `SURFACES.md:61,353,538` defer, `ACCESS.md` §10 delivers a three-state table. ✅
- **WebAIM Million, verified live at webaim.org/projects/million/**: "59.1 on average… 42 on average" ✅; "5.7% of home pages had an ARIA menu… 22% of those ARIA menus introduced accessibility barriers" ✅. The "~41% more" is correct arithmetic (59.1 ÷ 42 = 1.407) and matches WebAIM's own historical phrasing. Correlational-not-causal caveat carried.
- **Native-vs-web divergence** — §10 states it cleanly, both halves, with the "no principle reconciles them" conclusion.
- **Task 5 carry (icon-only naming)** — answered from the W3C Functional Images tutorial ("name the action, not the picture"), and the *measured cost* figure is separately and explicitly marked unverified (line 1343). Both halves handled.
- **18 name-from-content roles** — I re-fetched the APG page and counted: **18**, exact list, exact order as shipped. The report's 17→18 correction was real and is right.
- **600 tab stops** — 200 × 3 = 600. The 7,200 correction was real.
- **`§N` convention** — `grep -oE '\(§[0-9]+\)'` → **empty**. Broader sweep for any `§N` lacking backticks *and* lacking `above`/`below` → **empty**, except `§4.3` / `§4.3.1`, which are WAI-ARIA spec citations. All ten PRINCIPLES refs (`§6 §7 §8 §10 §11 §12 §13 §14 §15 §16`) map to the correct real sections.
- **No markdown links anywhere.** No links to unbuilt files; `loops/01-direction.md` and `DIRECTION.md` appear as backticked prose, which the brief itself mandates.
- **`./scripts/check.sh`** — placeholder scan clean, internal links resolve, ACCESS forks on surface class. 9 FAILs, every one naming a file a later task creates.

---

## Task quality: **Approved with two findings**

### Important 1 — one unhedged universal in the legal claim

`ACCESS.md:70`:

> **And no law in force names 2.2 either** (§12 below).

§12 gets the same claim right at line 1187: *"**No instrument verified here** names WCAG 2.2."* And the file's own unverified list, item 5, says: *"Any jurisdiction outside the US and EU. Not researched at all."*

So §1 asserts globally what §12 correctly scopes to three instruments. It's self-correcting two sections later and the design conclusion (2.2 is anticipatory, not compliance) is unaffected — but this is precisely the verified/remembered blur the project has been fighting, sitting in its highest-damage section. One-word fix: *"no law **verified here** names 2.2 either."*

### Minor 1 — the one leak, and it's in the SPA section

`ACCESS.md:672`:

> The default, in most frameworks, is that focus falls to `<body>`

Unattributed empirical claim about framework behaviour. Not in the provenance table; `grep -rniE "falls to .body|activeElement" docs/research/*.md` returns nothing. It happens to be true, but it is stated bare in the one section whose entire argument is that this area is unspecified. Hedge it or drop it.

### Minor 2 — report-only, no file impact

Report unverified-item 6 says the practitioner answers "are named as *not* being in any spec read" in the shipped file. They aren't named at all. The report's "and/or `legal-and-focus-verified.md`" phrasing technically covers it. Noting only because the shipped file is stricter than its own description — the safe direction.

**No Critical findings.**

---

## Ruling on size: **earned — do not split, and §12 is the wrong seam anyway**

Section line counts:

| §2 six criteria | §4 ARIA | §11 i18n | §10 native | §12 **the law** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **240** | 168 | 141 | 118 | **109** |

§12 is the *fifth*-largest section. Splitting it saves 8% of the file and buys a second file, a cross-link, and a sync obligation — the worst trade available. The implementer's instinct that §12 is the cleanest *conceptual* seam is right; it just isn't a size lever.

The real test is whether §12 is read on a different occasion from the rest. It isn't: §1 forward-references §12 explicitly at line 70, and a run asking "what is my accessibility target" reads them together. Splitting would break the one cross-reference that matters.

And the file is read on demand — `check.sh`'s resident budget check tests `AGENTS.md`, not this. 1,357 lines costs nothing at idle.

Density holds up under inspection: 240 lines carrying six criteria with normative quotes, five named exceptions, two scope corrections, and a geometry derivation is not padding. **Nothing should split or go.** If a budget ever forces a cut, the honest target is §2's per-criterion prose, not §12 — and I would argue against that too.
